en: The Ten Princes' Deeds: The First Book, the First Chapter.
He is the staff for the parasol of the cosmic egg, the stalk for the lotus-flower of the abode of Śatadhṛti (Brahmā),
the mast for the ship of the earth, and the banner-staff for the flowing stream of the celestial river (Gaṅgā).

May Your foot, which is the axle-rod for the wheel of light, the pillar-staff for the victory over the three worlds, the triple-stride of Śreya, and the rod of death for those who hate the gods, bestow prosperity upon us.

There is a city named Puṣpapurī, which serves as the touchstone for all cities; its greatness is proclaimed by the multitude of gems and other articles spread out for sale at all times, making it a veritable ocean of jewels; and it is the crown jewel of the Magadha country.

Therein, his towering staff-like arms acted as Mount Mandara for churning the ocean of the enemy host's camp— a sea made terrifying by its waves of heroic warriors, its crocodiles of horses and elephants; while he was being celebrated with songs of exceeding praise by throngs of young courtesans intent on sporting in the groves of Indra’s celestial courtyard— songs as white as the autumn moon, the kunda flower, camphor, frost, pearl necklaces, lotus stalks, swans, the elephant of the gods, water, milk, and the snowy mountain.

He was one whose fame—resembling the loud laughter of Kailāsa and filling the intermediate quarters of space—perfumed all directions; he was fortunate enough to enjoy the sovereignty over the beautiful Earth, who was girt by the shores of the oceans of radiant jewels upon the peaks of heaven;
and he was a multitude of Brahmins resplendent with the accumulation of distinguished learning, protected by the constant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) of his incessant sacrifices.

There was a king named Rājahaṃsa, whose majesty—causing constant torment to his enemies—constantly rivaled the swan in the midst of the sky; he possessed a charming and faultless beauty that was a sibling to the splendor of Kubera and Kandarpa.
He had a wife named Vasumatī, a woman of excellent disposition who was the crest-jewel of the Līlāvatī lineage.

When the mind-born god of love had been reduced to ashes by the eye on his forehead, which was harsh with rage, the faultless woman, out of fear, perceived him as a man of blameless character; she saw his mass of hair as a swarm of bees,
and his moon-like face, which surpassed the lotus, as a mine of affection.
The fish, appearing as a banner of victory, together with his wife, constitutes the pair of eyes;
the Malaya breeze, heroic in every limb of his army, is his breath;
and the coral, which is the sword for cleaving the hearts of travelers, is the orb of his navel-base.
Her neck is the conch of victory, possessing a graceful curvature and endowed with loveliness;
her two breasts are full jars resembling ruddy geese;
and her two arms, surpassing all others in softness, shine forth in splendor.
Her navel was like a whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, possessing playfully blooming *kahlāra* lily buds as its ornaments;
her victorious chariot, which surpassed the desires of yogis, was her exceedingly thick hips;
and her pair of thighs were like two pillars of victory, embodiments of beauty that obstructed the endeavors of those seeking self-restraint.
The thousand-petaled parasol became his two feet, while the other flowers became his remaining limbs, as if they had been transformed into weapons.
Residing in Puṣpapura, the city of the Conqueror of the Gods, Queen Vasumatī—cherished by boundless enjoyments—was experienced at her pleasure by the King of Magadha, as if she were the earth itself.

That king had three hereditary ministers named Dharmapāla, Padmodbhava, and Sitavarman, who were most obedient to him, whose intellects were so profound that they surpassed even the deliberations of the preceptors of the gods, and whose administrative affairs were characterized by literary excellence.
Of them, Sitavarman had two sons, Sumati and Satyavarman;
Dharmapāla had three sons, Sumantra, Sumitra, and Kāmapāla; and Padmodbhava had two sons, Suśruta and Ratnodbhava. Thus were their offspring born.
Among them, Satyavarmā, who was virtuous by nature, having realized the worthlessness of cyclic existence and desiring to go on a pilgrimage, departed for another land.
Devoted to courtesans and dancers, the ill-behaved Kāmapāla disregarded the commands of his father and elder brother and wandered the earth.
Ratnodbhava, too, by virtue of his skill in trade, made voyages across the ocean.
The other sons of ministers, when their fathers had become guests of Indra’s city, conducted themselves according to tradition.
START Dkc 1,1.12:

Then once, the Lord of Magadha—whose sharpened arrows were fixed upon the crest-jewels of countless kings and nobles by his skill with various great weapons; who was a devourer of fresh battles; and whose mental vigor was fierce—[marched] against Mānasāra, the lord of Mālava.

Accompanied by a fourfold army that surpassed the pride of the ocean’s roar with its playful, thundering din of kettledrums— a sound so harsh that it overwhelmed the fierce terror of those who heard it— and which possessed the strength to press down upon the heads of the serpent kings as the earth itself bent under its weight, he set forth, seized by a great fury born of his longing for battle.
The Lord of Mālava, too, accompanied by many leaders of numerous hosts, set forth once more with great resolve, appearing like the personified form of war itself.
Then,

as a mass of dust rose into the sky— stirred up by the earth trampled by the hooves of their chariot horses, its base washed by streams of ichor flowing from the temples of the herds of elephants, and appearing like a pavilion of curtain-cloths for the divine maidens who had come to choose new husbands— it spread across the expanse of the heavens.

The battle that ensued deafened the entire expanse of the quarters with the sound of drums that surpassed the cries of the gods, while the armies struck one another with weapon against weapon and hand against hand.
Thereupon,
the King of Magadha, having captured the King of Mālava alive after his entire circle of troops had been destroyed, reinstated him in his own kingdom out of compassion.
Then, ruling over the earth girt by the ocean as his unique domain, he, being childless, worshipped incessantly Nārāyaṇa, the sole cause of all the worlds.
START Dkc 1,1.17:
Now once, at the time of dawn, the chief queen beheld a fine dream, [in which she was told]: "O Queen, may you obtain the fruit of the wish-fulfilling creeper from the King. Dkc_1,1.17 //
Then she conceived a fetus that was like the flower of her beloved's heart's desire.

The king also, having surpassed Indra by his own splendor, summoned the circle of his friendly kings and celebrated the parting-of-the-hair ceremony for the queen in a manner befitting his own magnificence and his heart's desire.

Once, while seated upon his throne in the assembly hall with his well-wishing friends, ministers, and domestic priests, King Aśoka— who was not lacking in virtues— was informed by the doorkeeper, who stood with palms joined at his forehead: “O Lord,
a certain ascetic, whose mind longs for an audience with Your Majesty and who is worthy of being honored by Your Majesty, stands at the entrance.”
Permitted by him, that self-restrained man was led into the presence of the king.
START Dkc 1,1.22:

Having observed him approaching and having correctly discerned his status as a secret agent, the lord of the earth dismissed his entire retinue of attendants; then, accompanied by his ministers, he addressed the prostrate man with a gentle smile: "Surely, as you have been wandering through the country under various pretexts, you may relate whatever you have learned there. // Dkc_1,1.22 //
START Dkc 1,1.23:

He, powerful from his travels across the earth, addressed him with palms joined: “Your Majesty, having received your command upon my head, I have assumed this faultless disguise, entered the city of the Lord of Mālava, and while living there in great secrecy, I have learned the entire range of that king’s affairs.”
Having understood [this], he returned.
START Dkc 1,1.24:

The proud Mānasāra, having experienced defeat by you in battle—an obstacle to the longevity of his own soldiers—his heart marked by shame and devoid of compassion, propitiated the eternal Maheśvara, the dweller of Mahākāla and consort of Kālī; and from Him, gratified by the power of his asceticism, he obtained [the weapon] that slays the enemies of the peerless hero.
Having obtained the mace Bhayadā, Mahābhibhānu considers himself matchless and prepares to attack you;
beyond this, Your Majesty alone is the authority. Thus [he spoke].
START Dkc 1,1.25:

Having reflected on this, the ministers, having determined their course of action, informed the king: "Your Majesty, the enemy approaches to fight with no other means than by relying on Your Majesty as his ally."
"Therefore, war with us at this time is improper; we must immediately take refuge in a fortress."
Although entreated by them in many ways, the king, shining with unabated pride, disregarded their words as something not to be done and became intent on fighting back.
Mānasāra, whose essence was the power bestowed by Śitikaṇṭha, having assembled the equipment for battle and being fully equipped, entered the Magadha country without difficulty.
Then,

having heard that, the ministers somehow persuaded the great lord of the earth, the King of Magadha, and established his harem— protected by the core of his army— in the midst of the Vindhya forest, a place unassailable by enemies.
But the royal swan, accompanied by a praiseworthy army free from dejection, emerged with swift speed and hemmed in his enemy, who was filled with excessive rage.

START Dkc 1,1.30: While that battle was proceeding— a cause of wonder for the sky-dwellers who had come out of curiosity to behold it— between these two heroes who were bound by mutual enmity, the protector of the Mālava country, desiring victory, [encountered] him who, through his practice of steadfastness in various weapons, equaled the Lord of the Immortals in combat.
In former times, he hurled at that Lord of Magadha a mace given by the Enemy of Cities (Śiva).

Although she was shattered into fragments by a volley of sharp arrows, because the command of Paśupati is never in vain, she slew the charioteer and rendered the king, who remained in his chariot, unconscious.
Then, with their reins loosened and their bodies unhurt, the draft-animals, carrying the chariot by the power of destiny, entered the great forest that served as a refuge for the inner apartments.
The Lord of Mālava, accompanied by the Goddess of Victory, having seized the vast kingdom of Magadha, took up residence in the city of Puṣpapura.
There,

the ministers, exhausted by the repeated blows of those weapons, their lives sustained only by the course of destiny, having regained consciousness through the night breeze, somehow recovered their breath; but searching everywhere for the king and not finding him,
they approached the queen in their dejection.

But Vasumatī, having heard from them of the destruction of the entire army and the king’s disappearance, became agitated; submerged in an ocean of grief, she set her mind upon following her husband in death.
"O auspicious lady, death on this earth is uncertain.
Moreover, a charming and delicate prince, who has crushed and uprooted his enemies and is destined by the astrologers to be a universal monarch, dwells within your womb."
"Therefore, death today is unbecoming for you. Thus consoled by the ministers and the family priest with these adorned words, she, though deprived of her moment, remained silent for a moment.
Then, at midnight, while her attendants lay with eyes submerged in sleep and the surroundings were deserted, she— unable to cross the shoreless ocean of grief—
slowly traversed the camp area, which was devoid of even a trace of sound; there, because her chariot had become stuck, she was exhausted from the labor of bringing it out and fleeing.

Unable to proceed, the king’s horses stood for a while on the path, crowded with travelers; then, at the branch of a banyan tree standing nearby—as if it were a line marking death—those women, having fashioned a means of death by binding themselves with half of their upper garments, cried out with tearful throats, their own voices rendered harsh by the sweetness of his speech, as they desired to die: “O you who are compared to the flower-arrowed god of love in beauty!”
"O Lord of the Earth,
may you alone be my beloved even in a future birth."

Having heard that, the King of Magadha— having regained consciousness through contact with the mass of moonbeams, his movements lost due to the profuse flow of blood, yet certain of the Queen’s words— slowly called out to her,
uttering endearing words.

She came forward in a flurry of excitement, her lotus-face blossoming with intense joy in her heart; drinking him in with eyes that were unblinking as if they had been fasting for him, she called out loudly to the family priest and the ministers and showed him to them with a voice full of exultation.
START Dkc 1,1.40:

The king was addressed by his ministers, whose own lotus-feet were kissed by the foreheads [of their wives] and who praised the majesty of destiny: “Your Majesty, in the absence of the charioteer, the multitude of horses impetuously led the chariot into the forest. Dkc_1,1.40 //

"There, in that battle where the hosts of soldiers were slaughtered by the Lord of Mālava— who had propitiated the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva)— I was struck with a mace by that merciless man; having fallen into a swoon, I was awakened here in this forest by the evening breeze," so the king related.
Then,

by a group of ministers who had performed great rites and by a time that brought about divine favor, the king was brought to his camp; with all his arrows extracted and his own lotus-face blossomed, he was suddenly made to have his wounds healed.

The Lord of Magadha, whose human effort had been frustrated by adverse fate and whose appearance was pervaded by dejection, was fully awakened by that Vasumatī, who spoke with gentle words and was endowed with intelligence, through the consensus of his most eminent ministers.

"O King, while you are the most radiant and most venerable among the entire assembly of rulers, yet you dwell today in the midst of the Vindhya forest; thus, this glittering prosperity, which resembles a bubble on water, arises and perishes in an instant like a flash of lightning.
Therefore, having ascertained that everything is dependent solely upon destiny, one must act accordingly."

Furthermore, in the past, countless lords of the earth, headed by Hariścandra, Rāmacandra, and others— whose sovereignty was equal to that of Mahendra— fully experienced the machine of suffering that is the machinery of fate; after that, for many ages,
you too shall become just like them.
"Let him remain for a while, having composed his mind in divine concentration and being free from mental afflictions."
Then Rājahaṃsa, accompanied by his entire army, went to the ascetic named Vāmadeva, who was radiant with austerity, a treasure of penance, and the means for attaining his own desire.

Having prostrated before him and been received with hospitality by him, and having related all that was to be told, Mānasāra—the ornament of the lunar dynasty, a king among swans who speaks with moderation—dwelt for some time in that hermitage where all fatigue was dispelled.
Desiring his own kingdom, he said: "By the powerful force of destiny, Mānasāra has defeated me and now enjoys the kingdom that should have been mine."

"In the same way, I too, having performed severe penance, shall uproot that enemy by means of your compassion, which is a refuge for the world; thus have I come to you, who are observant of such vows.
Then the ascetic, who knows the three periods of time, said to the king: "Friend!"
"Enough with this asceticism that causes emaciation of the body!
A son of the king, who will crush the entire host of enemies, will surely be born from the womb of Vasumatī;
therefore, remain silent for some time."
Even with a voice moving through the sky, it was said: "This is true. The king, accepting the words of the sage, remained as he was.
Then, when her days of gestation were complete, Vasumatī gave birth at an auspicious moment to a son endowed with all the marks of excellence.

Placing before him a family priest who equaled Brahmā in spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), the king, skilled in his duties, named the delicate prince Rājavāhana, who shone with the performance of birth-rites and the ornaments of childhood.
He performed [the rite].

At that very time, to Sumati, Sumitra, Sumantra, and Suśruta— the ministers— were born sons of great renown named Pramati, Mitragupta, Yantragupta, and Viśruta, who possessed the luster of the newly risen moon and were long-lived.
Rājavāhana grew up, enjoying childhood sports together with the sons of the ministers, who were his own friends.
START Dkc 1,1.52:
Now, on one occasion, a certain ascetic, having presented to the king a delicate prince who was adorned with the marks of royalty and who brought joy to the eyes, said:
"O beloved of the earth, while I had gone to the forest to fetch *kuśa* grass and sacrificial fuel, I beheld a certain woman without refuge, openly shedding tears of wretchedness."
"O sage, why are you weeping in this desolate forest? When thus questioned, she wiped away her tears with her lotus-like hands and spoke to me in a faltering voice:
"O sage, [I am the daughter] of my friend, the King of Magadha, the Lord of Mithilā, who has surpassed the flower-arrowed god [Kāma] with his beauty and whose fame pervades the world of Sudharman."
Having arrived at Puṣpapura with his wife and children for the great festival of the parting of the hair,
and having propitiated the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), the sovereign of Mālava marched forth to wage war against the king of Magadha.

In that situation, while these two renowned men were engaged in an inconceivable battle, the King of Videha, Prahāravarmā— who was providing assistance to his friend with his own forces— was captured by a victorious enemy; however, he was released out of compassion and merit.
Accompanied by a depleted army, the survivors of the slaughter, he returned to his own city.

Then, as he was proceeding along a difficult forest path, Mahānirodha— whose harem was protected by his core forces— fled while being impetuously attacked by a superior force of Śabaras. I, who had been appointed as the nurse for his twin children, and my daughter were unable to keep pace with the king’s rapid movement.
There, a certain tiger with its mouth wide open, like personified wrath incarnate, quickly came to sniff me.
Terrified, I stumbled over a protruding rock and fell;
the child, slipping from my hands, hid himself in the lap of some brownish corpse.
A shaft released from the mechanical device of a bow snatched away the life-breaths of that intolerant tiger as it was dragging its prey; meanwhile,
even the child with dangling locks was taken up by the Śabaras and carried off somewhere.
"I do not know where my daughter has gone carrying another youth;

I had fallen into a swoon. Some compassionate protector of the Vṛṣṇis took me into his own hut and healed my wounds. Having then recovered, I wish to approach the presence of the Lord of the Earth, but I am hindered by being without a companion and by my ignorance regarding my daughter."
Saying, "I shall not be distressed," and declaring, "Even alone, I will go to my lord," she departed at that very moment.
START Dkc 1,1.57:

I too, experiencing despondency on account of the misfortune of your friend, the Lord of Videha, and searching for the prince who is the sprout of his lineage, once came upon a beautiful temple of Caṇḍikā.
START Dkc 1,1.58:

There, the Kirātas, intending to offer the prince as a sacrifice to the deity for the sake of constant victory of this kind, said, "We shall strike him down either with a sword while he hangs from the branch of a great tree, or by aiming at him with a volley of sharp arrows while his feet are buried in the sand, or by having him bitten by many young dogs as he flees on foot. To them, I replied: "O best of Kirātas!..."
In a wilderness of terrible conduct, having lost my way, I—an elderly Brahmin—left my little son somewhere in the shade and went a short distance to search for the path.
"Where has he gone? [I wondered].
"By whom has he been taken?
Even though we have searched, he is not seen; many days have passed without our beholding his face.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Was he not seen by you? [Dkc 1.1.59]
"O best of the twice-born,
does someone remain here?"
"Is this truly your son, Nandana?
Therefore, take him. Having said this, they bestowed him upon me through the favor of destiny.
Having received their blessing and having taken the boy under my care, I comforted him with treatments such as cool water and brought him here to your lap without hesitation.
May you, appearing in the form of a father, protect this long-lived one. Thus he spoke.

King [Kandarpaketu], having somewhat diminished his grief caused by the calamity that had befallen his friend through the pleasure of beholding his son, summoned him by the name Upahāravarman and nurtured him just like Rājavāhana.

START Dkc 1,1.63: On a certain auspicious day, as the lord of the people was traveling along the road near the hamlet for a ritual bath at a sacred ford, he beheld a certain boy of incomparable form being doted upon by some woman. Overcome with curiosity, he asked her: “O beautiful lady, whose joy to the eyes is this child—possessing such a lovely form and a perfection of royal qualities—is he not born of your own lineage?”
"Tell me truthfully, by what cause has he become dependent upon you?"
START Dkc 1,1.64:

Bowing down, that Śabarī spoke playfully: "O King, while the army of Śabaras was plundering the entire wealth of the Lord of Mithilā—who is equal to Indra and was traveling on the path near my own hamlet—this prince was seized by my beloved and handed over to me."
"He grew. // Dkc_1.1.64 //

Having understood that which was spoken by the sage, the king, who knew what ought to be done, determined that it was indeed the second prince; he then conciliated her with both conciliation and gifts, gave her the name Apahāravarmā, and handed him over to the queen, saying, "Raise him."
START Dkc 1,1.66:

Once, a disciple of Vāmadeva named Somadevaśarman, having bathed at Rāmatīrtha and returned, placed a certain boy before the king and said: "Your Majesty! While returning from bathing at Rāmatīrtha, I beheld this boy of radiant form being carried by some woman in a forest glade and addressed her respectfully: 'O old woman!'"
"Who are you? For what purpose do you wander with such exertion in the middle of this forest, carrying a young boy?"
Vṛddhā also spoke: “O best of sages,
on the island named Kālayavana, there is a certain wealthy and eminent Vaiśya named Kālagupta.”

To that Tannandinī, who brought joy to the eyes and was of excellent character, there came from this island a charming man named Ratnodbhava; born of the minister of the Lord of Magadha, a repository of delightful virtues, a traveler who had wandered the circle of the earth, he married her and was honored by his father-in-law with an abundance of excellent goods.
In the course of time, that woman of graceful form became pregnant.
Then Ratnodbhava, having somehow persuaded his father-in-law out of curiosity to see his sister, embarked upon a ship with Capalalocanā and set out for Puṣpapura.
The vessel, struck by a series of billows, sank into the waters of the ocean.
START Dkc 1,1.69:
Carrying that woman, who was languid from the weight of her pregnancy, in my hands as I had assumed the role of a nursemaid, I climbed onto a single plank and reached the shore by the turn of fate.
Whether Ratnodbhava, surrounded by his kinsmen, sank there or reached the shore by some other means, I do not know.

Having reached the very height of her affliction, this woman of virtuous conduct has today given birth to a son in the middle of this forest. Rendered unconscious by the pains of childbirth, she remains at the foot of a tree in the cool shade.

Since it is impossible to remain in this desolate wilderness, I have set out to search for a path leading toward a populated region; yet, thinking it improper to depart while leaving the infant near her as she is helpless, I [have left] the prince...
Thus he was led away as well.
At that very moment, a certain wild elephant appeared;
seeing it, she fled in terror, dropping the boy.
I remained hidden within a nearby thicket of creepers and shrubs, observing;
as the lordly elephant was about to swallow the fallen boy like a mouthful of young shoots, a lion pounced upon him with great ferocity.
Suddenly tossed into the air by the terrified elephant, the boy fell.

Because of his great longevity, he was seized by a certain monkey sitting on the branch of a lofty tree, which mistook him for a ripe fruit; having realized he was not a fruit, the monkey dropped him at the base of the trunk and then departed elsewhere.
That monkey, too, went off somewhere.
START Dkc 1,1.71:
By virtue of his perfection of courage, the young lion was cultivated to endure all afflictions;
having slain an elephant, he departed for some unknown place.

"Having emerged from the bower of creepers, I too slowly lowered the child—a mass of radiance—from the tree; searching for his mother within the forest and not finding her, I brought him here and presented him to my preceptor, and by his command, I have now brought him into your presence."
START Dkc 1,1.72:
Bearing a great wonder because the favorable turn of fate occurred for all his friends at once, the king, reflecting on how Ratnodbhava had come to be,
gave his son the name Puṣpodbhava and [related] his history.
Having explained it to Suśruta, and experiencing both sorrow and joy, he handed it over to his grandson.
On another day, Vasumatī, carrying a certain boy upon her breast, approached the beloved of the earth (the King).
When asked by him, "Where does this [boy] come from?", she replied: "O King!"

"Last night, a certain celestial maiden placed this boy before me and, awakening me from my sleep which was sealed by slumber, spoke with humility: 'O Queen, I am Tārāvalī, a Yakṣa maiden and the daughter of Maṇibhadra; I am the beloved of Kāmapāla, the son of your minister Dharmapāla.'"

"By the command of the Lord of Yakṣas, I have brought this son of mine to serve your future son Rājavāhana—who, surrounded by the earth girdled by the ocean, shall become a sovereign and a treasury of pure fame. Please nurture him, who is like the god of love himself.
Having been thus honored with humility by me, whose eyes were wide with wonder, that beautiful-eyed Yakṣī vanished from sight. Thus [he spoke].

Dkc 1,1.74: With his mind filled with wonder at the union of Kāmapāla with the Yakṣa maiden, Rājahaṃsa summoned his minister Sumitra, whose friend he had won over, and having appointed Arthapāla— the son of that minister’s brother— to the position, he explained the entire situation to him and gave it to him.
START Dkc 1,1.75:

Then, on the following day, a resident of that hermitage who was a disciple of Vāmadeva approached the king, bringing with him a certain boy—one whose splendor as a deity had been propitiated, whose form surpassed that of Māra, and who was as delicate as a flower—and said to him:
"Having placed a young child with disheveled locks upon the surface of my own lap and seeing an old woman weeping, I spoke: 'O old woman!'"
"Who are you? To whom does this child, who brings joy to the eyes, belong? For what purpose have you come to this wilderness?
And what is the cause of your grief?"
START Dkc 1,1.76:
Wiping away the tears with her two hands and looking at me as if I were capable of uprooting the very stake of her grief, she spoke of the cause of her sorrow: "O son of a twice-born!
Satyavarman, the younger son of Sitavarman, the minister of the royal swan-king, came to this country under the pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred fords."

Having married Kālī, the daughter of a certain Brahmin in a certain agrahāra, he found that she was childless; therefore, he married her sister, Gaurī, who possessed a golden luster, and through her he obtained a single son.
One day, Kālī, out of malice, took this boy along with me, his nurse, under some pretext and cast him into this river.

Lifting the child with one hand and swimming with the other, I clung to a branch of a certain tree driven by the river's current; having placed the infant there, I was bitten by a black serpent clinging to the tree as I was being swept away by the force of the flood.
The tree to which I was clinging reached the bank at this spot.
"Because the poison acts as an intensifier, once I am dead there will be no one in the forest to provide refuge; thus I am filled with grief."
Then, her limbs licked by the flames of virulent poison, she fell upon the surface of the earth.

My heart filled with compassion, yet unable to remove the agony of the poison through the power of mantras, I searched for a specific medicinal herb in the nearby thickets; having returned, I beheld that she had passed away.

Thereafter, having performed her funeral rites, his mind overwhelmed with grief, he took this helpless child and reflected that since the name of the village where Satyavarma resided had never been heard, it was impossible to search for him; thus, [he entrusted the child] to the son of your minister...
"Thinking, 'Only you can protect him,' I have brought him here to you."
Having heard that, King Satyavarmasthiti, his mind distressed by the uncertainty of the situation, entrusted Somadatta— the son of his younger brother— to his minister Sumati.
He too, regarding him as if he were his own returned brother, nurtured him with special care.

Thus, experiencing childhood sports with the assembled circle of princes and mounted upon many vehicles, Rājavāhana received in due order the collection of sacraments beginning with the tonsure and the sacred thread ceremony (*caula* and *upanayana*).

Thereafter, he attained mastery in the knowledge of all scripts, proficiency in the languages of all regions, and expertise in the entire corpus of the Vedas along with their six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

Proficiency in the Purāṇas along with poetry, drama, narratives (ākhyānaka), tales (ākhyāyikā), history, and illustrated stories; skill in the entire collection of sciences such as Dharma, grammar, astronomy, logic, and Mīmāṃsā; expertise in the compendiums of political science by Kauṭilya, Kāmandaki, and others; dexterity in all musical instruments beginning with the lute;
mastery in music, literature, and wit; cleverness in the manifold illusions of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs; and agility in riding mounts such as elephants and horses.

Having properly acquired from their respective teachers proficiency in the employment of various weapons as well as mastery in the deceptive arts such as thievery and gambling, the lord of the earth beheld that multitude of princes sporting in their youth and experienced intense, boundless joy, thinking, "I am one whom even my enemies find difficult to overcome."

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Birth of the Princes," in the *Daśakumāracarita* composed by the illustrious Daṇḍin. The Second Chapter. START Dkc 1,2.1: Then, having performed the auspicious rites for the birth of his sons, the king, accompanied by his queen, entered the inner apartments. There, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of Vedic hymns, he beheld his sons, who were like the rising moon and the sun, and felt as though he had attained the fulfillment of all his desires. He named them, after consulting with the astrologers and the elders of the city: Rājavāhana, Vijayavāhana, Nanda-vāhana, Śūdraka, Mantragupta, and Aparājita. As they grew up, they were instructed in the various branches of learning—grammar, logic, the arts, and the sciences of statecraft—and in the skills of archery, horsemanship, and swordsmanship. They became proficient in the use of weapons and the management of elephants, horses, and chariots. Thus, endowed with both physical prowess and intellectual acumen, the princes gradually attained their youth. Meanwhile, the king, having entrusted the governance of the kingdom to his ministers, devoted himself entirely to the pleasures of the harem. One day, while wandering through the pleasure gardens, he encountered a certain ascetic who was seated beneath a tree, surrounded by his disciples. The king, curious about him, approached and inquired, "Who are you, and what is the purpose of your penance? The ascetic replied, "O King, I am one who seeks liberation from the cycle of rebirth; I have come here to practice the yoga of self-restraint. The king, impressed by his composure, sat down near him and asked, "Tell me, what is the true nature of this world, and how may one attain eternal peace? The ascetic, perceiving the king’s noble disposition, began to discourse upon the nature of existence, the causes of suffering, and the path to liberation. He explained that all worldly pleasures are transient and rooted in illusion, and that true happiness lies in the realization of the Self. As the king listened, his mind was filled with a profound sense of detachment, and he resolved to renounce the throne in favor of his sons, seeking instead the life of a forest-dweller. Having made this decision, he returned to the capital and summoned his sons. He told them of his intention and asked for their counsel. Rājavāhana, the eldest, spoke with humility, "Father, the kingdom is our inheritance, and it is our duty to protect it. You should not abandon us to pursue a life of solitude. The other brothers agreed with him, pleading that they would remain at home and support their father in his old age. The king, moved by their devotion, relented and decided to spend the remainder of his life in the company of his family, dedicating himself to acts of charity and virtue. Thus, the kingdom remained in peace under the guidance of the ministers, while the king lived a life of contentment, surrounded by his sons and grandsons. End of the Second Chapter.

Then one day, Vāmadeva approached the king—who was surrounded by a multitude of princes whose hands were marked with the banners of victory, the sun-shade, and the thunderbolt; who were skilled in all arts; whose beauty rivaled that of the flower-arrowed god of love; who were as noble as if fashioned from his own essence; and who surpassed Kumāra in daring—and having accepted the service rendered to him by the king with bowed head, he [proceeded].
Having firmly embraced the multitude of princes— their side-locks acting like bees clinging to the pair of his own lotus feet, and their enemies about to be shattered—
he spoke, having offered them blessings with words of measured truth.
O Lord of the Earth, your son Nūtamitra enjoys a youthfulness of abundant loveliness that is like the very fruit of your heart's desire.
"Surely this is the time for the commencement of the world conquest of this prince, who is now accompanied by his companions.
Therefore, let the expedition for the world conquest of Rājavāhana, who is capable of enduring all hardships, be undertaken."

The princes— delightful to Māra, yet surpassing Rāma and others in prowess, having reduced their enemies to ashes with their wrath, and mocking the wind with their speed— rendered the king hopeful of victory through their martial expedition.
Having assigned them the role of his assistants and instructed them in appropriate wisdom, he dispatched the prince, along with his retinue, at an auspicious moment for the sake of conquest.
Observing auspicious omens that portended good fortune, Rājavāhana traversed a certain region and entered the heart of the Vindhya forest.

There he beheld a certain man whose body was marked by scars from weapons, whose frame was as hard as black iron, whose status as a Brahmin could only be inferred by his sacred thread, who possessed the manifest power of a Kirāta, and who was harsh to the eye.
Having received the worship thus offered, Rājavāhana spoke: "O young man,
why do you dwell alone in the midst of the Vindhya forest— a wilderness devoid of human company, frequented by wild beasts, and of terrifying passage?"
"The sacred thread brought by your hand reveals your status as a Brahmin;
yet, by the blows of weapons, the conduct of a Kirāta is inferred.
Tell me, what is this? (Dk 1.2.5)

Thinking, "This man, though possessing human form, is surely not composed of mere mortal prowess," that man learned his name and lineage from the mouth of his companion and related his own history to him: "O prince, there are certain people in this forest who, having abandoned the study of the Vedas and other sciences, cast aside their family traditions, and [neglected] the multitude of religious duties such as truthfulness and purity..."
Avoiding sin and seeking out that food, many who merely called themselves Brahmins lived there under the leadership of the Pulindas.

Among them was a son of one such man, named Mātaṅga, whose conduct was a vessel for reproach; accompanied by a force of Kirātas, I entered the countryside and, having brought wealthy men from the villages along with their women and children and placed them in captivity in the forest, I roamed about arrogant and pitiless, seizing all their wealth.
Once, in a certain forest, seeing a Brahmin being attacked by my group of companions, my heart overcome with compassion, I said: "O wicked ones, this Brahmin must not be killed!"
With eyes red with rage, they reviled me in many ways.
Unable to endure their harsh speech, I fought them for a long time to protect the guardians of the earth; struck down by them, I became one whose life had departed.

Then, having reached the city of the dead, I beheld Śamana seated upon a lion-throne inlaid with jewels in the midst of an assembly hall, surrounded by embodied men. I prostrated myself before him like a staff;
he, too, looked at me and summoned his own minister named Citragupta, and said to him: "Minister,..."
"This was not his time of death;
although he was of censurable conduct, he has become one whose life has departed for the sake of a Brahmin.
From this point forward, as his defilements have been washed away, a delight in performing meritorious deeds will arise within him."
"Having observed this particular torment being experienced here by the most wicked, let him return once more to his former body."

Citragupta also [beheld] those being bound there and there to heated iron pillars,
and those being cast into oil heated to an extreme degree within wide-mouthed earthen vessels.
Having shown me my limbs shattered by clubs and even being carved all over with sharp chisels, and having instructed me in the perception of merit, he released me.
I regained that very same former body and remained for a moment lying upon a stone slab, while a Brahmin minister, providing cooling treatments, attended to me in the midst of a great forest.
Thereafter, my circle of kinsmen, having learned of these events, came suddenly, brought me to their home, and healed my wounds.
A grateful brahmin, having provided me with instruction in the alphabet and taught me various scriptures and tantras, imparted that which is the cause for the destruction of all impurities.
Having instructed me in right conduct and explained the ritual for worshipping the moon-crested Lord— who is accessible through the eye of knowledge—
he accepted my worship and departed.
START Dkc 1,2.11:

Since then, having abandoned my circle of kinsmen who had formed associations with Kirātas, I dwell in this forest—having cast off all blemish—remembering in my heart the sole teacher of all the worlds, who is adorned by the crescent moon.
"Your Majesty, there is a certain secret that must be made known to you."
"Please come," he said.

On the bank of the river flowing through the heart of the Daṇḍaka forest, near a crystal linga worshipped by the Siddhas and Sādhyas, there exists a certain cave marked with the footprints of the Daughter of the Mountain King, resembling the very face of Fate.

Having entered it and taken up the copper plate inscribed therein— which is like a decree of the Creator— and having performed the rite prescribed thereon as if securing victory over Destiny, you, the sovereign of the netherworld...
"It must be so; the prince who is to assist you will arrive today or tomorrow.
Your arrival has occurred in exact accordance with that instruction.
"Render assistance to me, who desire the means of accomplishment and am intent on gratification."
"So be it," said Rājavāhana; and together with Mātaṅga, who bowed his head in salutation, he left his circle of friends—who were overcome by sleep at midnight—and entered another part of the forest.
Thereafter, his followers, searching for the prince throughout the entire night until dawn and not finding him, became despondent at heart and [searched] here and there...

Having thoroughly searched the forests and looking back no more, they departed from one another and went their separate ways— intent on the quest for this [truth], wandering through foreign lands, enduring great hardships, and having fixed upon a place for a future reunion.

Protected by the prince, the sole hero of the world, Mātaṅga’s inner heart was filled with contentment; having entered the cave without hesitation—its identity confirmed by the token mentioned by the Moon-crested Lord—he took up the copper charter and, proceeding by that very same path toward the netherworld (rasātala), arrived at a certain city there.

Near the lake in the pleasure grove where cranes were spread abroad, having performed a fire sacrifice with various kinds of oblations prepared according to the ordinances of the Lord’s command, and while Rājavāhana— whose obstacles had been averted— looked on with wonder at the blazing fire kindled with fuel and clarified butter,
she offered her body, the abode of merit, as an oblation preceded by mantras, and attained a divine form with a luster like lightning.
Thereafter, a certain maiden— adorned with a circle of jewel-encrusted ornaments, the very ornament of the entire host of women in all the worlds,

and followed by a modest retinue of many female companions— approached slowly with the gait of a swan; having arrived, she presented a single gem of radiant form as a gift to that best of earth-dwellers.
Thus questioned by him, "Who are you?", she, filled with longing, spoke very softly with her hands joined in reverence, her voice like that of a cuckoo.
START Dkc 1,2.16:
"O best of Brahmins,
I am Kālindī by name, the daughter of the foremost of Asuras."
"My father, the majestic ruler of this world, was made a guest of Yama’s city in battle by Viṣṇu, who could not endure his own prowess and drove away the gods.
Seeing me submerged in an ocean of grief at his separation, a certain compassionate perfected ascetic spoke to me:"
"O child, a certain young man possessing a divine body shall become your beloved and protect the entire netherworld.
Having heard that command, I stood for a long time longing for the sight of you, like a female cātaka bird facing the sound of a rain cloud while awaiting the arrival of the monsoon.

"Having understood that your arrival was becoming the fruit of my heart's desire, I have come to you with my mind acting as the charioteer of love, with the consent of the ministers who are the pillars of my kingdom. Having accepted the royal fortune of this world, may you make me its co-wife."

Mātaṅga, too, having married that young woman with the consent of Rājavāhana, was exceedingly delighted by the acquisition of a celestial lady; and having accepted the sovereignty of the netherworld (rasātala), he attained supreme bliss.
START Dkc 1.2.19:

Having deceived his circle of companions, Rājavāhana arrived there; desiring to travel upon the earth out of curiosity to behold it, he obtained from Mataṅga—who was gratified by his assistance—a jewel given by Kālindī that destroys the afflictions of hunger, thirst, and the like.
Having left him following the golden path, he emerged through that cave passage;
and there, beholding his circle of friends, he wandered over the earth.

While wandering in the outskirts of Viśāla, he reached a certain pleasure garden and, wishing to rest there, saw a man who had arrived at the park seated in a palanquin, accompanied by a beautiful woman and surrounded by trusted attendants.
His heart blossomed with supreme joy and the lotus of his face opened wide as he thought, "This is my lord Rājavāhana, the ornament of the Lunar dynasty and a treasury of pure fame."
"By my great good fortune, I have come to his very feet unexpectedly;

now a great festival for the eyes has occurred! Having said this, he descended from the palanquin in a flurry, and with a gait characterized by the playful grace of impetuous steps and an excess of joy, he advanced three or four paces and touched the pair of his lotus-feet with his head, from which a garland of jasmine flowers was falling and shimmering.

for all this time,
in what region..."
In what manner did you remain [there], where are you going now, and who is this young woman?
"How was this retinue acquired? Tell me."
He too, his intense fever of anxiety having subsided through the encounter with his friend, joined his lotus-like hands in salutation and spoke with humility concerning the manner of his own conduct.

START Dkc 1,3.1:
"O King, having become desirous of serving your lotus-feet, I was wandering when, overcome by thirst in a certain forest region, I drank from the cool water of a river surrounded by creepers.

There, I beheld a single gem of brilliant form. Taking it and traveling some distance, I was unable to proceed further due to the extreme heat of the sun; therefore, in this very forest, I [found] something..."
Having entered a temple, I beheld an elderly brahmin with a dejected face accompanied by many sons; moved by compassion and joy at his welfare, I questioned him.

With his face pale from wretchedness and his mind filled with hope for me, the Brahmin said: “O noble one, protecting these sons who are bereft of their mother by various means, I now dwell in this temple of Śiva, providing them with alms obtained in this wretched land.”

"O Brahmin, to what country does this king, the lord of this camp, belong, and what is his name?"
When asked, "What is the reason for his coming here?", the Brahmin replied: "Gentle sir,
the lord of Lāṭa named Mattakāla, having repeatedly heard of Vāmalocanā— the jewel among young women of incomparable beauty— who is the daughter of Vīraketa, the protector of this land,
besieged his city after that king had rejected his suit for her hand."
Vīraketu, too, being afraid, gave his daughter to Mattakāla as if she were a great gift.

The Lord of Lāṭa, his heart delighted by the acquisition of a young woman, decided that she must be married only in his own city; while returning toward his own country, he has now established a camp for his army in this forest out of a fondness for hunting.

Appointed by Kanyāsāra, the minister of Vīraketu named Mānapāla— whose wealth was his honor— having established his camp elsewhere and being accompanied by a fourfold army, pierced him from within, for his mind was distressed by the humiliation of his own lord.

"This man is a learned Brahmin with many sons, yet he is poor and elderly; he is worthy of a gift. With a mind full of compassion, I gave him a jewel.
With his face blossoming with supreme joy, the Brahmin departed for some destination after pronouncing many blessings.
Exhausted by the fatigue of the journey, I enjoyed the pleasure of sleep there.
Subsequently, that Brahmin, his pair of arms bound behind him and his body marked by the lash of whips, approached followed by many swordsmen and pointed me out, saying, "This is the thief."
The king’s soldiers, who had abandoned their Brahmins, disregarded my account of how the jewels were obtained and, having bound me— who was free from fear—
with tight ropes, brought me to the prison. Pointing out some who were already shackled, saying, "These are your friends," they likewise placed my pair of feet in fetters.

Stupefied as to what ought to be done and experiencing the anguish of despair, I said: "Surely these men are of heroic vigor; for what reason do you enter this insurmountable suffering of imprisonment?
These [guards] have designated you as their companions."
"What is this? he asked.

Having observed me in such a state, the thieves, after recounting to me what I had heard regarding the conduct of the Lord of Lāṭa, spoke again: “O noble one!
We are the servants of Mānapāla, the minister of Vīraketu.”

By his command, having entered the palace of the Lord of Lāṭa through a tunnel at night to slay him, we became despondent due to the absence of the king there; yet, having plundered much wealth, we entered a great forest. On the following day, many royal attendants searching for our tracks arrived, surrounded us on all sides as we held our hoard of wealth, bound us very tightly, and brought us nearby; then, during the time of the inventory of all the goods, because one priceless jewel was missing, [they prepared] for our execution.
"By giving us this ruby, they have indeed unchained us."

Having beheld the jewel among jewels that I had heard of, and having ascertained, "This is indeed that very ruby," I related my own wretched condition caused by the gift of land to a Brahmin, my birth and name, and the manner of my travels in search of you, using words appropriate to the occasion.
Through conversation, I established a friendship with them.

Then, at midnight, having broken our shackles along with theirs, and followed by them, I took the array of weapons from the sleeping guards at the gate and, with the playful ease of keen prowess, put to flight the city guards who came forward to confront me.
I entered the camp of Mānapāla;
having heard from his own servants the account of my family’s pride and my prowess at that time, Mānapāla honored me.

Thinking, "If this does not happen, a great calamity will arise," they spoke these most cruel words.
Hearing this, the minister, his eyes reddened with rage, asked: "Who is this Lord of Lāṭa, and what friendship can there be with him?"
He reviled them, saying, "What can be gained by serving this wretch?
And they reported to Mattakāla exactly those boastful words spoken by Mānapāla.
Although enraged, the Lord of Lāṭa, out of pride in his own prowess, advanced to do battle accompanied by only a small force of soldiers.
Having long ago resolved upon battle, the proud Mānapāla, having equipped himself as a warrior and desiring combat, went forth without hesitation.

I too, with great respect, took a chariot provided by the minister, equipped with many horses and a skillful charioteer; a very sturdy armor; a bow suited to me; two quivers filled with various arrows; and weapons appropriate for war.
Having taken him up, I followed the minister—who was intent on destroying the enemy and confident in my own strength—fully prepared for battle.

Having heard this entire account from one of Mānapāla’s attendants whom he had sent, the king was pleased in mind; filled with wonder at my prowess, he rose to meet me and, with the consent of his ministers and kinsmen, gave his daughter to me on an auspicious day amidst great festivities.

"Experiencing happiness, yet with a heart easily pierced by the thorn of the pain of separation from you, I have today arrived here together with my wife to propitiate the Supreme Lord dwelling in Mahākāla— a place whose fruit is the sight of my kinsmen, according to the instruction of a Siddha.
Through the compassion of Gaurī’s husband, who is affectionate toward his devotees, I have obtained a flood of bliss from beholding the lotus-feet of your venerable self."
Having heard this, Rājavāhana—his prowess celebrated and his mind reproaching fate for the punishment inflicted upon one who was innocent—related his own life story to him in due order.

At that moment, beholding Puṣpodbhava before him, he hurriedly embraced him firmly as the latter touched the toes of his feet with the surface of his forehead and joined his palms in reverence; meanwhile, Rājavāhana’s eyes blossomed wide, clouded by tears of joy.
"O gentle Somadatta,
this is that Puṣpodbhava," he said, and showed him to him.

Having cast off the sorrow of their long separation, the two of them experienced the pleasure of embracing one another.
Then, sitting in the shade of that very tree, the king spoke with a respectful smile: "Friend,..."
"Thinking that my circle of friends, having learned the matter, would create an obstacle in every way as I was intent on performing the service for the Brahmins, I departed, leaving you all asleep.

With his cupped hands touching the surface of his forehead, he also spoke with humility:

"Your Majesty, although my circle of friends was certain that Your Majesty had departed solely for the sake of assisting the king of the earth, being unable to determine the specific region to which Your Majesty had gone, they separated from one another and went forth in all directions to search for you.

I too, while wandering the earth in search of Your Majesty, once, unable to endure the rays of the sun as it reached the middle of the sky, sat for a moment on the cool shade at the foot of a tree on a mountain slope."
In my presence, beholding a human shadow in the form of a tortoise with all its limbs contracted as if at midday,

I looked up and saw a certain man falling from the expanse of the sky with great velocity; moved by compassion even while he was still in mid-air, I caught him, gently laid him upon the ground, and having revived him— who had lost consciousness due to the long fall— with cooling treatments, I found his eyes filled with tears from the excess of his grief.
I asked him the reason for his leap from the cliff.
START Dkc 1,4.3:
Wiping away the teardrops with his fingertips, he also spoke:
"Gentle sir, I am Ratnodbhava by name, the son of Padmodbhava, the minister of the Lord of Magadha."

Having traveled to the island of Kālayavana in the guise of a merchant and married a certain merchant’s daughter, he was returning with her when his ship was wrecked in the ocean not far from the shore; as everyone else drowned, he somehow reached the land by the favor of destiny, and while floating in an ocean of grief caused by separation from his wife, he acted out of respect for the instructions of a certain perfected ascetic (siddhatāpasa).
"Having somehow passed sixteen years while not looking for the end of my suffering, I threw myself from a mountain."

At that very moment, a certain cry of lamentation from a woman was heard: "Truly, this is not fitting— that you, unable to endure separation, should enter the fire when union with your fallen son has been ordained by the Siddhas."
Having perceived through my mind that he was my father, I said to him: "Father, there are many things to be reported to you;
let it be so."
"Afterwards, everything shall be related;
for now, I must not disregard the cry of the woman.
Please stay for just a moment."
Thereupon, I proceeded for some distance with haste. There,
before me, I saw a woman with her hands joined in a gesture of reverence, who had undertaken the audacious act of plunging into a fire filled with terrifying flames.
Seeing someone, I hurriedly removed her from the fire and, having led her along with the cackling old woman to my father’s presence,
I said to the elder woman: “Old lady, where are you two from?”
"By what cause is such a miserable state being experienced in this wilderness?
Tell me."
START Dkc 1,4.7:
She spoke with a faltering voice: "Son, she is the daughter of a certain merchant named Kālagupta on the island of Kālayavana; her name is Suvṛttā, and she was given [in marriage] by Ratnodbhava."

While returning with my own husband, the ship sank in the ocean; grasping a single plank together with my nurse, I reached the shore by a stroke of fate. Having reached the time of my imminent delivery, I gave birth to a son in a certain forest. But due to my misfortune, when the child was seized by a wild elephant of the woods, I, accompanied only by my nurse, wandered about until sixteen years had passed.

"Thinking, 'There will be a reunion with my husband's son,' she spent that time in a certain holy hermitage out of faith in the words of the perfected ones; then, unable to endure her boundless grief, she prepared to offer her body as an oblation into the blazing fire."

Having heard that, and recognizing her as my own mother, I prostrated before her like a staff, related my entire story to her, and presented my father, whose face was blossoming at the nurse’s words and whose eyes were wide with wonder.

Recognizing one another through these tokens of identity, the two parents, their inner selves filled with joy, sprinkled me— who was humble before them— with a rain of tears of bliss, embraced me firmly, and, smelling the crown of my head, sat down in the shade of a certain tree.
START Dkc 1,4.9:
When asked by my father, "How does the royal swan, the beloved of the earth, dwell?", I related to him his fall from the kingdom,
your birth, the acquisition of all the princes, your commencement of the world-conquest, and our pursuit of the Mātaṅga.
I explained to you the entire reason for my search;
thereafter, I established those two in the hermitage of a certain sage.
Then, intent upon searching for Your Majesty and having determined the wealth required for all purposes, [I acted] through the favor obtained from you.
Having prepared a group of disciples skilled in assisting the practitioner, they went to the sites of ancient cities within the Vindhya forest; there,
having identified with *siddhāñjana* jars filled with wealth buried beneath various indicator trees,
and while guards stood all around, they unearthed them with digging tools, piled up countless *dīnāra* coins, and [placed them] not far away, where some had arrived at that very moment.

Approaching a certain encampment of merchants that had been established there, I purchased strong oxen and sacks; under the pretext of other goods, I had them slowly transport that wealth accumulated in the sacks back to the camp.
Thereupon, having formed a friendship with a certain merchant’s son named Candrapāla who was authorized to act on my behalf, I entered Ujjayinī together with him.

After escorting my parents to that city as well, I was led by his father, Bandhupāla—who is a repository of all virtues—to an audience with the Lord of Mālava; and with his permission, I took up a secret residence there.

Then, having heard that I was intent on searching for you throughout the forest lands, my dear friend Bandhupāla said: “Since you are unable to search the entire surface of the earth—which is without end—abandon your mental exhaustion and remain silent.
Once I have observed an auspicious omen that will lead to the sight of your lord, I shall tell you.”

I am ready to assist you.
My composure was shaken by her loveliness, and I became a target for the arrows of the flower-tipped shafts of the god of love.
START Dkc 1,4.12:

She too, whose eyes were like those of a startled young fawn, having gazed at me repeatedly with a sidelong glance that acted as an arrow for the flower-arrowed god of love, trembled like a creeper shaken by a gentle breeze.
Through particular glances—turned inward by her mind, slightly contracted, hovering between passion and shame, and darting across her limbs—she revealed the state of her own heart.

Having correctly understood her heart's affection through four types of secret gestures, I reflected upon a means for our happy union.

On another occasion, Bandhupāla, desiring to observe your movements by means of birds, approached the pleasure grove on the outskirts of the city with me and remained there, listening to the cries of the birds from beneath a certain tree.

While wandering through the depths of the forest, intent on diverting my longing, I beheld Bālacandrikā—the sole ground of my desires—on the shore of a lake, her mind overcome by anxiety and her face downcast.

Experiencing the pleasure of her playful glances— charming with agitation, love, bashfulness, and curiosity— he, wishing to know the cause of the dejected state upon the lotus-face of that fair-toothed woman, which was experienced due to the exhaustion of being overwhelmed by love, playfully [inquired].
Approaching her side, I said:
"O fair-faced one, tell me the cause of this dejection regarding your lotus-like face."

Having cast aside shame and fear due to the confidence born from their secret intimacy, she spoke softly: "Gentle sir, Mānasāra, the sovereign of Mālava, because of the great onset of old age, has consecrated his son Darpasāra as ruler in Ujjayinī."
