let it be so, listen.
Is it not the case that for one who disregards dharma, neither wealth nor pleasure can arise?

Dharma alone, independent of those [other goals], is the cause for the production of the happiness of cessation (*nivṛtti-sukha*), and it is to be accomplished solely through the stabilization of the self (*ātma-samādhāna*).
It does not depend excessively upon external means such as wealth and desire.
Furthermore, when reinforced by the vision of reality (*tattva-darśana*), it is not obstructed by wealth and desire even when practiced in whatever manner possible.
Even when obstructed, if one remedies that obstacle with little effort, one may eliminate even that fault and be fit for great spiritual welfare.
For example: the desire of the Grandfather (Brahmā) for Tilottamā, and the sight of the Lord of Bhavānī (Śiva) of thousands of sages’ wives.
The sixteen-thousand women of Padmanābha’s harem indulging in dalliance; Prajāpati engaging in amorous advances even toward his own daughter; and Śacīpati being a paramour to Ahalyā.
The moon’s violation of his teacher’s bed, the sun’s transgression against the mare,
and the wind’s union with the wife of the lion.
Bṛhaspati’s pursuit of Utathya’s wife,
Parāśara’s violation of the fisherman’s daughter,
and Pārāśarya’s union with his brother’s wife.
In this regard, the union of Atri’s son with a doe,
and the deceptions of the Asuras against the gods in their various affairs, do not bring about any injury to Dharma due to the power of knowledge.
And in a mind purified by Dharma, no stain of passion ever adheres, just as dust does not settle upon the sky.
"Therefore, I believe that neither wealth nor pleasure touch even a hundredth part of dharma.
Having heard this, the sage, whose passion was aroused, replied: "O playful one, you see rightly; for those who perceive the truth, dharma is not obstructed by the enjoyment of sense objects."
"But from birth we have been ignorant of the affairs of wealth and desire;
moreover, what are these two like in form, what is their retinue, and what is their fruit?
She replied: "Wealth, first of all, consists of acquisition, increase, and preservation."
The retinue of desire consists of agriculture, animal husbandry, trade, peace, war, and so forth, as well as the fruit of establishing sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Desire, however, is a particular kind of contact that provides unsurpassed pleasure to a man and a woman whose minds are intensely attached to sense objects.
Its retinue includes everything in this world that is delightful and brilliant.

Furthermore, the fruit is supreme delight, born from a succession of mutual friction; it is sweet when remembered, unsurpassed, characterized by an awakened sense of self-identity, immediate, and directly self-evident.
For his sake alone, those dwelling in exalted positions endure hardships,
perform great acts of charity,
and engage in fierce battles.
"Men perform even such formidable deeds as crossing the ocean," he said.
Having heard this, whether by the power of destiny, through his own cleverness, or due to the dullness of his own intellect, he disregarded his own restraint and attached himself to her.
She, having led that deluded soul a great distance by ship, brought him to her own residence via the royal highway of the city, which was of magnificent splendor.
And an announcement was made: "Tomorrow there shall be a festival of love.

On the following day, having bathed and anointed himself, wearing beautiful garlands, and having begun the conduct of a lover—his own duties abandoned and tormented even after a mere moment had passed without her—he was led by [the king] along the prosperous royal highway to the festive assembly.

In a certain grove, in the presence of the king who was surrounded by hundreds of young women, she was commanded by him with a smiling face, "Noble lady, sit down with the Blessed One," and having performed her salutation with graceful charm, she sat down with a smile.
Thereupon, a certain excellent woman rose up with palms joined in reverence and said, "O King..."
"I have been conquered by her;
from this day forward, I accept servitude to her," she said, and prostrated before her lord.
A tumultuous clamor, rooted in both wonder and joy, arose among the people.

Having been favored by the delighted king with precious jeweled ornaments and a great retinue, and being praised in groups by the chief courtesans and the leading citizens, she went to her own residence; yet even before arriving, she offered this salutation with joined palms:
"This servant has long been favored."
"Now you must attend to your own interests.
But he, as if struck by the thunderbolt of passion, spoke distractedly: "My dear, what is this?
Whence comes this indifference?"
"Where has your extraordinary affection for me gone? she asked.
Then, with a smile, she replied: "Venerable sir, today I was insulted by her when she said to me, 'In some contest between her and me, you boast as if you had won Marīci over from me.'"
"Out of a bond of friendship, I engaged in this matter;
and by your grace, I have achieved my purpose.
Having spoken thus, that wicked-minded man, treated with such contempt, remained like one in a desolate forest, filled with remorse.
O noble one, consider me to be that very ascetic whom she has thus made;
having extracted the passion infused by my own power, a great dispassion has been instilled in him by that very forest-dweller.
Before long, it will be possible to make this self capable of accomplishing your purpose.
"In this very city of Campā, the abode of the Vasus.
Then, as if out of fear of the touch of the darkness that had fallen upon his mind, the sun went to its setting;
and the passion released by the sage manifested itself as the twilight.
As if their passion had been extinguished by his discourse, the lotus groves closed their petals;
you, having followed the sage’s instruction, performed your twilight devotions together with him and passed the night conversing with him on appropriate topics.
Then, as the rays of the dawn—resembling a forest fire on the mountain of sunrise and surpassing even the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree—began to break forth, the night drew to a close.
Having paid homage to him, I departed for the city.

On the way, near a certain monastery of the Kṣapaṇakas, I saw a certain Kṣapaṇaka seated in a secluded grove of red Aśoka trees outside; he was not yet touched by meditative absorption, appeared exhausted, was the foremost among the unattractive, and possessed a wretched complexion.
And I observed drops of tears falling from his mouth onto his chest, loosening the accumulation of dust upon it;
then, sitting near him, I asked: "Where is penance, and where is weeping?"
"If it is not a secret, I wish to hear the cause of your grief. He replied, "Gentle sir, listen.
I am named Vasupālita, the eldest son of a merchant named Nidhipālita, in this very city of Campā."
Because of my deformity, I was known as "The Ugly One" (*nirūpaka*).
There was another man there named Sundaraka, whose name was true to his appearance; he was richly endowed with artistic skills and virtues, yet not overly wealthy.
On account of our respective bodies and wealth, a rivalry was instigated between him and me by certain rogues among the citizens who live off such enmities.

Once, at a festive assembly of ours, they themselves pacified a verbal dispute rooted in mutual contempt that had arisen between us, and established this rule: "Neither physical form nor wealth is the basis of manhood;
rather, he who possesses youth coveted by the most excellent courtesans is truly a man.
Therefore, let him whom Kāmamañjarī—the ornament of young women—desires take her as his prize of good fortune."
Having agreed, we both dispatched messengers to her;
it was said that I alone had been the cause of her madness of love.
While we two were seated, she approached me and, casting upon my body a garland of side-glances as if made of blue lotuses, she made that man cast his face downward in shame.

Thinking myself fortunate, I made her the mistress of my wealth, my home, my circle of followers, my body, and even my life; yet she reduced me to nothing more than a beggar’s bowl of refuse. Having stripped me of all my possessions, she cast me out, making me an object of public derision. Unable to endure the reproaches of the city elders, I have now found solace here in this Jaina monastery, where a certain sage has taught me the path to liberation—a path that is easy to follow.
Thinking, "This is indeed the dress of those who have gone forth from the household," I, having aroused a fervent dispassion, did not abandon even that coarse garment.
However, with my body smeared with scattered filth and mud, suffering the intense pain of forcibly plucking out my hair, and enduring the extreme misery of hunger, thirst, and the like,
I was agitated by powerful restraints even in standing, sitting, lying down, and eating— like a newly captured elephant— and thus I reflected.
“I am a twice-born;
this descent onto the path of heretics is not my own dharma.
My ancestors proceeded only by the path ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti.”

"But for me, unfortunate as I am, this path of unrighteousness—which possesses a censurable appearance, is a great abode of suffering, and yields the fruit of hell even after death due to the constant habit of listening to slanders against the deities such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha; which consists mostly of deception and is utterly fruitless—had to be practiced by me as if it were dharma.
Thus reflecting upon his own misconduct, having reached this secluded cluster of trees, I shed a sufficient amount of tears.
Having heard this, I spoke out of compassion: "Good man, forgive me;
dwell right here for a short while.
I shall strive so that this very courtesan may provide for you by means of her own wealth."

"There are such means," he said, and having thus comforted him, I did not rise. As soon as I entered the city, I learned from public rumor that the city was filled with greedy and wealthy people; demonstrating the perishable nature of material wealth and restoring them to their natural state, I formed this intention regarding the son of Karma: "Having sent forth my son, I shall act in such a way that he will not return again. Thus I resolved. Then, having summoned the son of Karma, I spoke these words: "O son of Karma, you who are skilled in the ways of the world, listen to me. This city is full of those who are greedy and possessed of great riches. You must go there and, by means of various stratagems, bring about the destruction of all those who are greedy for wealth. Once they have been destroyed, you may return here at your pleasure. He replied, "I shall do so. Having given him leave, I dismissed him. And when he had departed, I remained here alone, awaiting his return. But even now, after a long time has passed, he has not returned. Therefore, I have come here myself to see what has become of him. "If he has perished, I shall enter the fire; if he has returned, I shall embrace him. Thus I thought, and so I have come. O King, if you know where he is, please tell me. If he has returned, I shall embrace him; if he has perished, I shall enter the fire. Therefore, O King, tell me where he is. Hearing this, the king was filled with wonder and spoke these words: "O Brahmin, you are indeed a man of great power and wisdom. You have performed a most difficult task. I shall tell you where he is. Go there and bring him back. "Very well," he replied, and taking leave of the king, he departed. And as he went along, he saw a certain man who was emaciated, pale, and suffering from disease. Seeing him, he asked, "Who are you? Why are you in such a state? He replied, "I am the son of Karma. I was sent by my father to destroy the greedy and wealthy people of that city. But while I was there, I became infatuated with a certain woman, and through that attachment, I lost my resolve. I have returned here, defeated by passion. Hearing this, the Brahmin reflected: "Alas! Passion is indeed a powerful enemy. Even one such as this, who was once firm in his purpose, has been overcome by it. Therefore, I must take care to guard myself against passion. Thinking thus, he approached the king and said: "O King, I have seen your son. He is indeed alive, but he is overcome by passion. I shall bring him back, but I fear he will not be able to fulfill his father's command. Nevertheless, I shall try. The king said, "Bring him back quickly. If he returns, I shall grant him whatever he desires. "Very well," he replied, and setting out, he reached that city. There he saw the son of Karma, who was living in luxury with that woman. Seeing him, he approached him and said: "O son of Karma, why have you abandoned your father's command? Have you forgotten your duty? He replied, "I have not forgotten it. But passion is too strong for me. I cannot fulfill my father's command. The Brahmin said, "Passion is a transient thing. It arises and passes away like a flash of lightning. Do not be deluded by it. Return to your father and fulfill his command. If you do not, you will surely suffer the consequences. The son of Karma said, "I shall go. But first, let me see this woman one last time. "Do so," said the Brahmin, and having led him to her, he returned to the king. And when he had related everything that had happened, the king was deeply moved and spoke these words: "O Brahmin, you have done a great service. I shall grant you a boon. "I desire nothing else," he replied, "except that you should protect your son from the power of passion. "So be it," said the king, and having honored the Brahmin, he dismissed him. And the son of Karma, having been brought back, was instructed by his father and eventually attained liberation. Thus ends the story of the son of Karma. It is told to show that even the wise are subject to the power of passion, and therefore one must always be vigilant. Thus I have related this tale to you, O King, to illustrate the impermanence of worldly things and the necessity of guarding against the passions. May you be victorious! May you be prosperous! May you live long! May you attain the highest bliss!
Thus I pray. And with these words

Having entered the gambling hall, I associated with the fraudulent gamblers. I observed their skill in all twenty-five varieties of gambling arts, as well as their expertise in the dice-board, the hands, and other implements; furthermore, I witnessed their extremely subtle fraudulent maneuvers, the arrogant insults rooted therein, and their utter disregard for their own lives.

He experienced these and other things: the agitated movements [of the players], legal proceedings based on the testimony of the master of the gambling hall, the predominance of logic, force, and majesty, the inability to achieve one's objective through mere acceptance [of the rules], conciliations toward the powerful, threats toward the weak, skill in forming factions, various kinds of inducements, descriptions of the different types of stakes, generosity in the distribution of wealth, and the frequent, incessant clamor of the crowd.
I attained satisfaction and laughed at a certain gambler who had played with some negligence;
but the opponent gambler, as if burning me with a gaze copper-red with anger, looked at me and said, "You are teaching the ways of gambling under the pretext of laughter!"
"Let this wretched man remain untrained;
I shall play against you alone, O wise one," he said, and with the consent of the superintendent of gambling, they exchanged their positions.
And I defeated him for sixteen thousand dīnāras.
Having given half of that to the master of the hall and to the members of the assembly, and taking the other half for myself, I rose up;
and there arose among those present words of praise filled with joy.
Furthermore, out of deference to the wishes of the master of the hall, I partook of a most magnificent meal in his house.

And he who was the root cause of my entry into the gambling hall—my companion named Vimardaka, who was like a second heart to me and more trustworthy than my own—had, through his own mouth, ascertained the entire city in its essence, its activities, and its character. Then, dressed in dark blue garments and a loincloth, appearing as black as the darkness stained by the throat of Śiva (Dūrjaṭikaṇṭha), and girding a sharp sword at my waist, I set out equipped with many implements: a whistle shaped like a serpent’s mouth, pincers, a human head, magic powder, magic wicks, measuring lines, compasses, ropes, lamps, and a basket for bees.

Having gone to the house of a certain wealthy man and broken into it, I entered the interior unobserved through a fine hole in the wall made by a cloth-burning lamp, as if entering my own home; then, taking a great amount of the finest property, I departed.
On the royal highway, which was thickened with darkness dense as a mass of dark clouds, I suddenly perceived a flash of light for a moment, like the sudden appearance of lightning.

Then, like the tutelary deity of the city dwelling within that urban wasteland, a certain young woman emerged at a time when there was no crowd; she appeared nearby, her ornaments beginning to gleam. "Who are you, lady? Where are you going? he asked her with compassion. She replied, her voice faltering with fear: "Noble sir, there dwells a most excellent nobleman named Kubēradatta."

I am his daughter. As soon as I was born, my father gave me in marriage to a certain merchant's son named Dhanamitra, a resident of this very place. That father of mine, out of extreme generosity, has—by means of his own wealth—effectively purchased poverty from the class of supplicants, leaving them destitute.

When my father— who had bestowed upon me the further, praiseworthy name "Satyathodāraka" because of the affection of the world— was about to choose me for him, yet, thinking me too young and myself lacking wealth, he wished instead to give me to another merchant named Arthapati (whose name was indeed appropriate), I realized that this ill omen would surely come to pass at dawn. Therefore, having already made an appointment with my beloved and deceived my own kin, I have set out by the path I practiced in childhood to go to his house as one who hastens to meet her lover.
"Therefore, release me;
take this vessel," she said, and having unfastened it, she offered it to me. Feeling compassion, I said: "Come here, virtuous lady."
"I shall lead you to your beloved's dwelling," I said, and took three or four steps forward.
Then there approached a large force of elephant-riders, their hands grasping staffs and swords, as the mass of darkness was being dispelled by the light of their torches.
Upon seeing them, I spoke to the trembling maiden: "My dear girl, do not fear!"
"I have this second arm of mine; however, this gentle means has been devised out of consideration for you.
I shall lie down, manifesting the symptoms of the onset of poison.
You, too, must say these words: 'We entered this city at night.'"
"And this husband of mine has been bitten by a hooded serpent in this corner of the assembly hall;
if there is anyone among you who knows mantras and is compassionate, let him restore him to life so that he may save the life of me, who am protectorless.
Then that young woman, having no other recourse, her voice faltering with fear, her eyes clouded by a rain of tears, and trembling all over, somehow managed to go and carry out my instructions.

And having thus reflected, someone among them—whose nature had been transformed by the cultivated poison, who possessed the conceit of being a master of medicine, and who, having attempted to treat me with seals, tantras, mantras, meditations, and so forth, had failed to achieve his purpose—declared: "This man bitten by the snake is already dead;
for indeed, his limbs are rigid and dark, and his vision is obstructed."
"The heat has indeed subsided; enough with this grief, Vāsuki. Tomorrow we shall consign him to the fire."
"Who can overcome destiny? saying this, he departed along with the others.
Having risen, I escorted her to Udāraka and said: "I am some thief;
with my mind fixed solely upon you and acting as your companion, I intercepted this woman as she was coming toward you and, out of compassion, brought her to your side."
"This is her ornament," he said, and offered that as well, which had torn asunder the mass of darkness with its web of rays.
Udāraka, however, taking it, spoke to me with shame, joy, and agitation: "Noble sir, by you alone has this beloved of mine been given to me on this night."
Furthermore, my speech has been taken away from me;
for this reason, I do not know how to say that this deed of yours is wonderful. Your own character does not appear wonderful to me.
"Nothing of this kind has ever been done by another," thus the power of things is indeed restricted;
for greed and the like belonging to others do not arise in you.
That "virtue has been manifested by you today" is generally not pleasing when compared to your previous noble deeds.
"To say, 'This servant has been purchased by you with this merit,' is to purchase what is utterly worthless for something of great value; that is an insult to your wisdom.
To claim, 'This body is the repayment for the gift of my beloved,' is to imply that when she was lost, this body—which was already destined for death—was given by you as well.
Or rather, this much is appropriate in this matter."
"From this day forward, this servant is to be protected by you," he said, falling at my feet.
Raising him up and embracing him to my chest, I spoke: "My good man, what is your plan for today?"
He replied: "I cannot live here having married her without the permission of my parents;
therefore, this very night I intend to leave this country. Who am I, that I should act as you command?"
Then I said: "That is true;
for a wise man, there is no calculation of 'one's own country' versus 'another country.
However, this girl is of no small delicacy."
The paths through the wilderness are arduous and abound with perils;
by such an abandonment of one's country, some slight weakening of both wisdom and fortitude might be occasioned by this misfortune.
Therefore, it is better to dwell here comfortably together with her.

"Come, let us take her to our own dwelling. With his consent granted without hesitation, I immediately brought her to that house; then, with her acting as our scout, we plundered everything there except for the earthenware vessels. Having escaped from there and deposited the stolen goods somewhere, as we were setting off, we encountered a group of city guards on the road. Seizing a certain intoxicated elephant-driver lying by the side of the path, we pulled him up onto the back of the animal and mounted it.

And as I was being raised up by him, whose pair of feet were caught in his neck-ornament, he— having struck down the elephant-driver and having his tusks entangled in the creeper-like intestines protruding from the broad chest of the fallen driver— destroyed that force of guards.
We two then demolished the house of Arthapati with that very [elephant],
and having carried it away to a certain dilapidated garden, we descended by clutching the tips of the branches.
When the two of them had returned to their own home, bathed, and were reclining upon their beds with the splendor of lords,
at that very moment the orb of the sun rose from the ocean— resembling a ruby on the peak of the king of the Eastern Mountains, rosy like a cluster of golden sprouts from the *kalpa* tree.

Rising, having washed their faces, and having performed the auspicious morning rites, as we wandered through the city bustling with our own business, we heard a great clamor in the houses of the bridegroom and the bride.

Then Arthapati, having consoled Kubēradatta with wealth, arranged for the marriage of Kulapālikā with a one-month deadline. In private, however, he instructed Dhanamitra thus: “Friend, attend upon the King of Aṅga in a secluded place, presenting this leather bag containing a jewel.”

And tell him: "Your Majesty surely knows me as Dhanabhī, the only son of Vasumitra, whose wealth amounts to many millions. Having become a squanderer of my capital, I have been treated with contempt by the class of creditors.
Because of the fault of my own poverty, although a maiden of noble family was raised up for my sake, she has been given again by Kubera-datta to Arthapati as his daughter."

Driven by despair at being about to be given away, I plunged into an old forest near the city to abandon my life; there, with a sword placed against my throat, I was stopped by a certain matted-haired ascetic who spoke thus to me: "What is the root of this rash act of yours?
I replied: "Poverty, which is the brother of contempt."
Then that compassionate one favored him further, saying: "Father, you are deluded.
There is nothing more wicked than the abandonment of oneself. The virtuous rescue themselves by not allowing themselves to sink."
There are many means for acquiring wealth, but not even one for the recovery of a life whose throat has been severed. What is the use of this?
I am one who has attained mastery over mantras.
This leather-sack jewel, which holds a hundred thousand measures, has been accomplished.

For a long time, through its grace, I dwelt among the Kāmarūpas, granting the desires of my subjects. Now, having entered this region of earthly heaven while still in my envious old age, I have come here.
Please accept this;

for it is the common understanding that this [cow] yields milk for others besides me—namely, for merchants or for the chief courtesans. However, that from whose side anything has been unjustly taken must be returned to him.
"However, wealth acquired through righteous means should be offered to the gods and the Brahmins.
Now, this leather bag, like a deity, has been placed in a pure spot and worshipped; every morning it appears as if filled with gold.
This bag, being a jewel itself, was brought here because it must not be used for one's livelihood until it has been offered to the god."
"But the god is the authority.
And the king will certainly say this: "My good man, I am pleased; go!"
"Enjoy this as you wish," he said.
Furthermore, say: "May she be protected in such a way that no one robs her.
He will certainly agree to that as well.

Then, having returned to your own home, you should carry out the relinquishing of wealth as previously instructed; by filling [the vessel] every night with wealth obtained through theft and displaying it to the public in the morning while performing worship day after day, Kubera-datta—being greedy for wealth—will disregard Arthapati like a blade of grass and will himself approach you with his daughter. Then, Arthapati, becoming enraged, will, out of pride in his wealth, bring a lawsuit against you to litigate the matter.
"Furthermore, we shall reduce him to nothing more than his loincloth by various clever means; in this way, our own theft will remain perfectly concealed.
Delighted, Dhanamitra carried out exactly as he had been told.
On that very day, at my command, Vimardaka became intent on serving Arthapati and increased his enmity toward Udāraka.
Then the greedy Kubēradatta, having desisted from Arthapati, sought to offer his daughter to Dhanamitra with conciliatory words;
however, Arthapati rejected him.

During these very days, it was announced that Kāmamañjarī’s younger sister, named Rāgamañjarī, would perform a musical concert at Pañcavīra’s pavilion; consequently, the city-dwellers gathered there with great enthusiasm.
I too, along with my friend Dhanamitra, took my place there.
And when she began her dance, my mind became a second stage for the performance.

And the five-arrowed god, taking refuge in the true bow of the forest of blue lotuses that was her flickering gaze, pained me excessively—as if his strength had been fully aroused by the conjunction of all the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*). Then she, like a city goddess dwelling in a city parched by drought, bound me with the chains of her garlands of playful side-glances, dark as the petals of the blue lotus.
And rising from her dance, she who shone with the attainment of supernatural power said: “Is this out of sport?”
Whether it was out of desire or simply by chance, I do not know.
Having looked at me repeatedly with sidelong glances that were unnoticed even by her friends— glances accompanied by the playful arching of her creeper-like brows—
and having smiled slightly under some pretext, revealing the moonlight of her teeth, she departed,
followed by the eyes and minds of the people.
Thus, having returned to my own home, with all desire for food cast aside by an irresistible longing, I lay upon a secluded couch with my limbs relaxed, making the pretext of a headache.
And Dhanamitra, who was highly proficient in the arts of love, approached me and said in secret: “Friend, that very courtesan’s daughter is truly blessed;”
Whichever woman my mind thus does not settle upon,
and whose disposition toward existence I have well discerned—
even her, the god with five arrows will soon lay down upon the bed of arrows.
Furthermore, the union of one who is fixed in his place and one who is intent on departure is to be accomplished with great effort;
however, that courtesan girl, by her noble and magnanimous disposition which opposed the customary duty of harlots, declared: “I am to be won by virtue as my price, not by wealth.”
"And youth is not for enjoyment by another apart from the taking of the hand in marriage.

Having repeatedly forbidden this, her sister and Mādhavasenā, the mother of Kāmamañjarī, with throats choked with tears, petitioned the King: "Your Majesty, our hope was once very great—that your maidservant Rāgamañjarī, possessing a character and skill in the arts commensurate with her beauty, would fulfill our desires; but today that hope has been cut off at its root."
"If she disregards her own family dharma and, indifferent to wealth, wishes thus to sell her youth for the sake of virtues alone, and intends to follow the unswerving conduct of a noble woman—
if she would even return to her natural state at the command of Your Majesty’s feet, then it would be well.
And although she was thus instructed by the king in accordance with his request, she remained entirely unheeding.
Then her sister and mother, through persistent weeping, petitioned the king: "If any libertine should, against our will, deceive and ruin this girl, he shall be put to death like a thief.
This being the case, her father consented to the marriage provided it was not for money.
"But he will not agree to give us the wealth; therefore, we must consider a stratagem for this. Then Māyā said, "What is there to consider here?
Having won her over with our virtues, let us secretly satisfy her kinsmen with wealth."
Then, having won over a certain Śākya nun named Dharmarakṣitā, who was Kāmamañjarī’s chief messenger, by providing her with robes, alms-food, and other gifts,
I made a wager through her with that harlot: “I shall give you the jewel of a deer-skin after I have stolen it from Udāraka, provided that Rāgamañjarī is returned as the counter-payment.”
When she had thus consented, and while Rāgamañjarī— intoxicated by the excellence of the qualities I had produced for that purpose— was overcome with passion, I took her sprout-like hand.

On the night when the rumor of the theft of the skin-jewel began, and when the leading citizens had been summoned under the pretext of another business and were listening, my spy Vimardaka, having assumed the name Arthapartigṛhya, bypassed Dhanamitra and provoked him greatly.
And Dhanamitra said: "My good friend, what purpose do you have that you revile me for the sake of another?
I do not recall even the slightest harm done to you by me."
He spoke again, as if threatening him: "This is what is called the pride of wealth—that you wish to win back by means of money from her parents the wife of another who was purchased for a price.
And yet you say: 'What injury have I done to you?'"
Is it not well known that "Vimardaka is the very life-breath of the merchant Arthapati moving outside his body"?
Therefore, for his sake, I would even give up my life;
I would not shrink even from the murder of a Brahmin.
“This fever of pride regarding my precious skin-jewel is the remedy for my single night of wakefulness,” he said.
As he spoke thus, he was restrained with indignation by the city leaders and led away.
Meanwhile, this news was reported to the king by Dhanamitra, who feigned distress and had already introduced the subject of the loss of the skin-jewel at the very beginning.

But, suddenly awakened by that calamity which instantly stripped me of my pride, I reflected with an insight born at that very moment: "Alas!

And since Rāgamañjarī has become my possession,

Again, I said to my mother: "In this very manner, you too must attend upon this queen with undivided devotion.
And whatever occurs there day by day, you alone must inform me;
furthermore, let this Kalpasundarī follow her like a shadow, for she is destined to bring about the fulfillment of our future karma, which is sweet in its final result."
And he carried out that matter exactly as instructed.
After some days had passed, my mother said to me, "Child,
I have established her in such a way that she considers herself wretched, like a *mādhavī* creeper clinging to a neem tree."
"What more remains to be done?
I replied, "I shall paint my own likeness and send it to her;
once she has received it and gazed upon it, she will certainly speak thus."
“If she asks, ‘Is there indeed any man of such a form? answer her: ‘If there were, what of it?
Whatever her reply may be, I must be informed of it.”
Saying "So be it," she approached the royal palace and, upon her return, informed me in private: "My child, that painted canvas was shown to that elegant lady;
and as she gazed at it, she remarked, 'This world has truly found its protector, for even in the god whose bow is made of flowers, such splendor of form is not present.'"
This is a marvel, a most wonderful marvel!
And I do not know who it is that creates such a thing here in this world;
by whom has this been painted?
Having spoken thus, she showed her respect;
and I, smiling, replied: "Queen, you command what is fitting."
It is impossible even to conceive that the Blessed One, whose banner is the makara, could be so beautiful;
nevertheless, this girdle of the ocean is vast,
and by the power of destiny, even such a form might exist somewhere.
"But if some youth were present here, of such a form, possessing skill, character, learning, and knowledge corresponding to his beauty, and born of a noble family—
what would he receive?
She replied, "Mother," and so on.
"What shall I say?
This body, heart, and life—all of it is insignificant and unworthy.
Therefore, nothing at all will be gained [from me], unless there is some deception; rather, you should show favor so that, through the experience of seeing her, this eye may become fruitful."
Furthermore, in order to make [my case] more certain, I proposed: "There is a certain prince wandering in disguise.

During that spring festival, you came by chance within the range of his vision as he was sporting in the city garden with his female companions, like Rati herself incarnate. And he, having become the sole target for the arrows of Kāma, has been following me."

And I, urged on by our mutual suitability—unattainable for others—in matters such as appearance and in the excellence of our virtues, have long worshipped you with flower-garlands, ointments, and other offerings fashioned by myself; furthermore, having myself painted this likeness, I have sent it so that you might perceive the intensity of my absorption in you.
If this matter is certain, then for him, whose life-force, courage, and excellence of wisdom are superhuman, nothing indeed is difficult to accomplish.
“I shall show him this very day;
a signal must be given.
Having reflected upon this for a moment, she spoke again: “Mother, ...”
This is not something to be kept secret from you now;
therefore, I shall tell you:
my father shared a great friendship with King Prahāravarmā.
My mother’s dear friend was Queen Priyaṃvadā.
While they were both yet childless, they made an agreement: “The son of one shall be given to the daughter of the other.
But my father, by a stroke of fate, gave me away to Vikaṭavarman—who had lost his own children and was entreating for one—when I was born, under the pretext that he was seeking Priyaṃvadā.

Moreover, this husband of mine is cruel, treacherous toward his father, lacking proper physical proportions, unskilled in the arts of love, with little interest in the fine arts such as poetry and drama, intoxicated by his own valor, boastful, a liar, and one who rains insults out of place;
he does not please me at all, especially on these days when he— having become intimate with me in the garden— [acts thus].
Disregarding even Puṣkarikā, who stood nearby and was envious of me due to my shared status as a co-wife, he— lacking self-knowledge and acting like a character in his own drama—
decorated with his own plucked flowers Campakalatā, whom he had raised as if she were his own child, though she was named Ramayantika.
On the jeweled terrace within the interior of Citrakūṭa, which had been enjoyed and vacated by me, he sported with her.
An unworthy man has thus proceeded with contempt.
Why, then, should one regard the fear of the next world when it is already obscured by the suffering of this life?
For those whose hearts have become quivers for the arrows of the bodiless god of love, the suffering of being constrained by living with an undesirable person is indeed unbearable.
Therefore, let this man meet me today in the Mādhavī bower of the garden.
For my mind has become excessively enamored with him merely by hearing his name.
"There exists this mass of wealth;
having established him in this position and having provided for him excessively, I shall live [upon it].
Having agreed to that, I have returned.
"Beyond this, the prince is the authority.
Then, having learned from her very presence the layout of the inner apartments, the positions of the eunuchs, and the various sections of the pleasure grove,
the orb of the sun turned crimson, as if its blood were stirred up by its fall upon the peak of the western mountain.
The mass of smoke from the embers of the sun, extinguished by being cast into the western ocean, seems to expand as darkness fills the sky;
while the moon, the foremost of planets, has risen— praising its own great consort as if to act as my preceptor in my desire to seize another's wife—

and while the Lord, eager for world-conquest, has his splendor fanned by the smiling orb of the moon, which resembles the lotus-face of Kalpasundarī appearing at first out of her excessive passion upon seeing me.
I took to a bed that was appropriate for the occasion and reflected:
"This matter is already as good as accomplished;
however, by violating another's wife, there may be an injury to dharma."
Moreover, the attainment of both wealth and pleasure is indeed sanctioned by the authors of the scriptures.

Furthermore, this transgression was committed by me through a strategic alliance aimed at securing my release from the bonds of my elders; may that very act, having expiated my sin, endow me with even a small portion of merit.
However, having heard this, I was overcome by sleep while lost in the thought, "What indeed will King Rājavāhana and his friends say?
And in a dream, the Blessed One with the face of an elephant appeared; he said:
"O gentle Upahāravarman,..."
Let there be no such ill-conceived thought in you,
for you are a portion of me;
this woman of excellent complexion is the celestial river, worthy of being cherished within the mass of Śaṅkara’s matted locks.

Once, unable to endure my agitation, she cursed me, saying, "Go to the state of a mortal! And I was cursed by her, saying, "Just as you were enjoyed by many here, so even after attaining human birth, become common to many! Yet she entreated me, saying, "Having had only you as my husband before, may I enjoy you alone for as long as I live."
"Therefore, this matter must indeed be regarded by you as free from doubt.

Having awakened, I spent that day also filled with joy, recollecting the details of my beloved's assignation and other such matters. On the following day, the bodiless god of love, whose conduct was unchanging, rained down his arrows upon me alone.
The lake consisting of light belonging to the luminous one dried up, and the mire consisting of darkness spread abroad;
and there appeared one clad in garments of mud, with his retinue more firmly arrayed, sword in hand, and the necessary equipment for the task brought forward.
Recalling the tokens given by my mother, I approached the moat surrounding the royal palace, which was filled with water up to its brim.

Then, at the gate of my mother’s house near the excavation, I took the weaver’s shuttle that Puṣkarikā had previously placed there; using it as a lever, I lay across the moat, and with it propped against the wall, I scaled the rampart.
Having ascended, I descended to the ground by a flight of stairs constructed of baked bricks that led up to the upper level of a gateway.
Once descended, I passed through the Bakula alley and, having proceeded a short distance along the path of the Campaka row, I heard to the north the piteous cry of a pair of ruddy geese.
Then, moving toward the north for the distance of an arrow-shot along a path of Pāṭala trees, whose interior was formed by the walls of spacious mansions reachable by touch, I went on.
Again, having proceeded a short distance further north along a sandy path whose two sides were adorned with groves of *piṇḍī-bhāṇḍīra* trees,
I entered once more a mango avenue leading southward.
There, I beheld a *mādhavī* vine bower, its interior made more secluded by a raised jeweled altar, which was revealed by the light of a lamp-wick emerging from a slightly opened casket.

Having entered, I opened the door— which was made of a branch of a red *aśoka* creeper fallen to the ground, marked by the thrill of fresh flower buds, and rosy with a mass of tender new shoots— and entered the inner chamber, which was enclosed on one side by a wall consisting of rows of young *kuraṇṭaka* shrubs densely covered with blossoming flowers;
there lay a well-spread bed of flowers.
The golden pitcher was filled with articles for correspondence;
having sat down and rested for a moment, I smelled an exceedingly intense fragrance and heard the very soft sound of footsteps.
As soon as I heard this, I emerged from the trysting-house and stood with my slender body concealed by the side of a red *aśoka* tree trunk.

That fair-browed woman, whose desire was intense, approached slowly; not seeing me there, she was deeply distressed and uttered a voice faltering yet melodious like the cry of a rutting royal swan: "Clearly, I have been deceived."
There is no means to remain alive.
O heart, why do you, having resolved upon this improper act as if it were a duty, thus weary yourself because of its impossibility?
O Lord Pañcabāṇa!
"What offense have I committed against you that you burn me thus, yet do not reduce me to ashes?
Then I appeared before him with the vessel of my lamp uncovered and said, "O beautiful woman,"
Surely you have committed a great offense against the Mind-born God, in that Rati— his very life-breath— has been eclipsed by your form;
his bow-staff by your creeper-like eyebrows, and his string made of a row of bees by the luster of your dark tresses.
He [overcame] weapons with showers of sidelong glances;
the silk banners of his standard dyed with saffron with the networks of rays from his teeth;
and the Malaya breeze, his first friend, with his fragrant breath.
She was a cuckoo through her exceedingly sweet warbling; a banner made of flowers through her staff-like arms;
and a pair of full jars for the commencement of a world-conquest through the pair of jars that were her breasts.
The lake of ritual action [is represented] by the circle of the navel; the chariot of armor by the circle of the hips;
and the pair of jeweled archway pillars of the celestial palace by the pair of thighs.
With its playful ears like young shoots and with the radiance from the soles of its feet,
the god whose banner is the fish torments you even while you remain in this very place;
yet that he exhausts me, who am innocent, all the more— this alone is his fault.
"Therefore, be gracious, O beautiful one;
revive me, who have been bitten by the serpent of Love, with your side-glances that are like life-restoring herbs," he said, and embraced her.
And I took my pleasure with her, whose large eyes were charming with the passion of love.

Perceiving her— her purpose accomplished, her eyes reddened and rolling, the roots of her cheeks marred by the emergence of slight lines of perspiration, uttering unrestrained cries of lamentation, engaged in the pitiless application of her teeth and nails, and with her limbs exceedingly relaxed as if in distress— I slackened both my mental and physical concentration and made myself one with her in purpose. At that moment, having abandoned all restraint, we remained for a while experiencing the rites at the conclusion of lovemaking, like long-acquainted friends who have attained deep intimacy.
Again, sighing hot and long breaths, with a somewhat dejected gaze, I embraced her gently with my arms outstretched with trepidation and kissed her not very clearly.
But she, with a tearful face, said, "O Lord, if you depart,
consider my life as already departed."
"Take me as well; otherwise, this servant will be of no use. Thus she brought her hands together in a gesture of reverence.
And I said to her, "O innocent one,"
"What conscious person would not welcome a woman who desires him?
If your intention is fixed on favoring me, then act without hesitation upon my instruction:
show the king in private a painted canvas containing my likeness."
"And tell me, has this form reached the ultimate limit of human beauty, or not?
"Certainly it has," he will surely say.
Speak further: "If that is so..."
There was a certain female ascetic who had gained confidence through wandering in foreign lands and who had become like a mother to me.

She presented me with this painted image and said: "There exists such a mantra by which you, having fasted on the day of the lunar festival, alone at night in a secluded place before the sacrificial fire into which oblations have been offered by the priests, [should offer] a hundred sticks of sandalwood."
Having offered a hundred sticks of aguru, a handful of camphor, and abundant silk garments as oblations, you will come to possess such a form.
Then, you shall ring the bell;
and when your husband, summoned by the ringing of the bell's cavity, reveals all his secrets to you and embraces you with eyes closed—if this occurs, [you will succeed].
"This form shall pass over to him;
but you yourself shall remain exactly as you were before, provided this pleases both you and your beloved,
and no deception is to be practiced in this matter."

“‘This form of yours is so highly esteemed that, having deliberated with your friends, ministers, younger brothers, and the people of both city and countryside, you will surely proceed with this undertaking once they have given their consent.
He will certainly agree.

Then, in this very same bower at the edge of the pleasure grove, having offered a consecrated animal according to the Atharvan rite, when the Fire has been released and I have entered it as a column of smoke, right here—”
"You must stay in the vine-arbor;
you, however, at the deep hour of nightfall, with a playful smile made upon your ear, shall address Vikaṭavarman thus: 'You are a rogue and ungrateful!
Even with this beauty, obtained through my favor, which serves as a festival for the eyes of the world, you will take pleasure in my rivals.'"
"I will not perform the raising of a Vetāla for my own destruction.
Having heard these words of yours, you shall come alone and report to me whatever he says; after that, I myself will know what to do.
Furthermore, have Puṣkarikā erase the marks of my footsteps in the grove.

Saying "So be it," she honored my words as if they were the instruction of a teacher; yet, with a passion for amorous delight that remained unsated, she entered the inner apartments with great difficulty.
I too, having departed by the same way I had entered, returned to my own dwelling. Then that beautiful woman carried out that matter exactly as instructed.

That evil-minded man remained steadfast in that view, and this wondrous report spread among the citizens and country-folk: "It is said that King Vikaṭavarman, through the power of the queen's mantras, will attain a body fit for a god;
surely this is a deception, not a very auspicious one."
What need is there to mention negligence?
This matter was indeed to be accomplished by his own chief queen within the very garden of his inner apartments;
for it was deliberated upon and approved even by ministers whose intellects were equal to those of Bṛhaspati.
"If this is indeed so, there is nothing else more wonderful than this;
for the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is truly inconceivable"— as these popular rumors spread, on a festival day,
at the hour of nightfall when the thick darkness was deep, a column of smoke, grey like the throat of Śiva, rose up from the palace garden.
The fragrance of oblations of milk, clarified butter, curd, sesame, white mustard, fat, meat, and blood wafted with the wind in every direction.
When that rising of smoke had suddenly subsided, I entered, and she,
who moved with the gait of an elephant, went to the palace garden.
And embracing me with a smile, he said, "O rogue,
what you desired is accomplished; and this sacrificial animal is finished."
To entice him, I spoke according to your instructions: "O gambler, I do not acknowledge your beauty;
for if you were as handsome as this, you would become an object of envy even for the Apsarases."
"How much less so for human women?
A cruel man like you, as naturally fickle as a bee, becomes attached to anyone and everyone.
But he, falling at my feet, said: "O lady with thighs like plantain stalks,"
"Endure the misdeeds committed by me;
from now on, I shall not even think of anything else in my mind. Hasten in the task at hand."
Therefore, I have approached you in such a bridal attire;
even before this, she—this wife endowed with virtue and beauty—was already given to you by the bodiless God of Love, with the fire of passion as witness.

Now, once again, having made this Jātavedas (the Fire) my witness, she is given by my own heart. Saying this, she pressed the top of his foot with her forefoot, lifted her heel, and [embraced him] with her soft, petal-like fingers interlaced with one another.
Wrapping her two vine-like arms around my neck and playfully tilting my face upward, she herself raised her lotus-face and, with wide, wandering eyes, kissed me repeatedly.

Then, dismissing her with the words, "Stay right here within the thicket of *kuraṇṭaka* shrubs while I go out and properly accomplish what needs to be done," I approached the site of the sacrificial fire and [found her] hanging from a branch of an *aśoka* tree.
I rang the bell,
which remained silent as if summoning that person with the messengers of Death;
and I began to offer oblations of aguru, sandalwood, and other substances.
The king arrived at the place as described;

looking about with some astonishment and appearing somewhat apprehensive, he stood there, and I said to him: "Speak the truth once more to me, even with the venerable Citrabhānu himself as your witness:
if you do not delight my co-wives in this form, [I shall know your intent]."
"Therefore, I shall transfer this form into you.
At that very moment, having gained a clear conviction that "this is indeed the queen herself, not a disguise," he proceeded to take an oath.
Smiling, I spoke again: "What need is there for an oath? For what mortal woman indeed could ever despise me? If you consort with the apsarases, [then you may do as you wish]."
"Unite with me as you desire;
tell me what your secrets are,
for at the conclusion of that telling, your true nature will surely perish."
He said: "My father's younger brother, Prahāravarmā, is imprisoned.
It has been resolved by the ministers that I should kill him with poisoned food and then proclaim it to be a case of indigestion.
The army is intended to be given to my younger brother Viśālavarman for an expedition against the Puṇḍra country."

The city elder Pāñcālika and the caravan leader Paritrāta consulted with me in private, saying that a single diamond, worth the entire earth, was obtainable from a Yavana named Svanati for a very small price. Furthermore, the householder Śatahalin, who is a close associate of mine and a great man of the district, said: "I shall have the wicked village headman Anantasīra—who is arrogant and of a habit of speaking falsehoods—put to death by inciting a popular uprising against him. Thus, they spoke regarding the matter of executing those who bear the rod of punishment.
"He agreed to employ me for this purpose.
Thus, this secret has been recently introduced.
Having heard this—"Such is the extent of your life," [he said].

"Go to the destination appropriate for your own karma! Having said this, I cut her in two with a knife and offered the mere fragments, as soon as they were severed, into that very fire of Hiraṇyaretas where the abundant clarified butter was flowing.
And she was reduced to ashes.

Then, having comforted my beloved wife—who was somewhat distressed due to her feminine nature—and taking hold of her sprout-like hand, I went to her house; and by her permission, having summoned all the women of the inner apartments, immediately—
Thus I rendered service.

Having spent some time in the midst of a circle of astonished courtesans, I dismissed the assembly of women of the harem; then, embracing that very woman of shapely thighs—pressing her thighs together and clasping her with my arms—I delighted her upon the couch and passed that night as if it were but a short moment.
And from his mouth, I learned the character of that royal family.
Having bathed at dawn and performed the auspicious rites, I met with the ministers and said to them: "Noble sirs,..."
My very nature is such that it revolves together with form itself.
He who was intended by me to be killed by poisoned food shall instead release this kingdom of his to me and have it restored once more;
we shall attend upon him with nothing but service, just as we did our father.
"For there is no sin greater than the murder of one's father.

And having summoned his brother Viśālavarman, he said: "My son, the Puṇḍras are currently not well-supplied with food; struck by misery and delusion, they may abandon their lives and attack our kingdom, which is not yet prosperous."
"Therefore, you shall march forth only when a pestilence or a crop-failure occurs; a campaign today is not appropriate.
I also spoke thus to the city elders: "Let it not be that for the sake of protecting the Dharma, a highly precious object is obtainable by me at a very small price."
"Let this be purchased for a price consistent with that," he said.

Then, having summoned Śatahali, the chief of the realm, he declared: "As for that Anantasīra who was intended for destruction because he was on the side of Prahāravarmā—even he, while my father remains in power, why should he be destroyed?"
"Therefore, you too must not harbor any resentment toward him.
Having perceived all these supernatural signs, they concluded, "This is indeed he," and filled with wonder,
they praised me and the Great Queen, extolled the power of the spells, and having released my parents from their bonds, [they departed].
They restored their own kingdom to me.
And I, having had all these deeds of mine made known in secret to my parents by that nurse of mine, took refuge at the feet of them both as they reached the pinnacle of joy;
and with their permission, I enjoyed the glory of the position of crown prince.
Having adorned myself and, while experiencing pleasures made wretched by the sorrow of being separated from your Majesty’s feet, I learned from a letter of this Simhavarman— my father’s friend—

that Caṇḍavarman was preparing an expedition against Campā. Thinking, "The slaying of an enemy and the protection of a friend are both indeed duties to be performed," I set out with a vast army that was swift to mobilize.
"And there was no lack of the great festival of joy from the direct realization of the splendor of your feet upon this earth.

Having heard this, King Rājavāhana spoke with a smile: "Behold, even an illicit affair involving deception, though it be so, has brought about abundant wealth and merit, as it served as the cause for liberating my elders from a calamity, as a means for the destruction of a wicked enemy, and as the root for the acquisition of a kingdom."
"For what indeed, when employed by an intelligent person, does not attain beauty?
Having cast a tender, long glance upon the face of Arthapāla, he commanded: "May you relate your own life story.
He too, with palms joined in reverence, spoke:

**Chapter Four** START Dkc 2,4: Caturthocchvāsaḥ (The Fourth Chapter)
"Your Majesty, wandering with these very friends through the circle of the earth— which is garlanded by the waves of the single ocean— I once approached the city of Kāśī, Vārāṇasī.
Having performed ablutions in the waters of Maṇikarṇikā, which are as pure as broken jewels, and having bowed down before the Lord Avimukteśvara, the slayer of Andhaka,
I was circumambulating him when I beheld a certain man of immense stature, his loins girt by arms as thick as iron clubs, his copper-colored eyes swollen from incessant weeping."
And I reflected: "This man is harsh; his eye has a wretched, starved look even after so many years, and his undertaking betrays a reckless nature.
Surely, indifferent to his own life, he will undergo some great hardship rooted in the calamity of a beloved person."
Therefore, I shall question him;
if there is any opportunity for me to provide assistance, I will approach him and ask: "Good sir, this armor betokens a venture of great daring."
"If you will not tell me, I wish to hear the cause of your grief. He gazed at me with great respect and said, "What is the harm?
Let it be heard."
Once, seated at the foot of a *karavīra* tree together with me, he told this story: “Noble sir, I am that very person;

formerly, as one who acted according to his own will, I was a householder’s son named Pūrṇabhadra. Although raised with great effort by my father, I followed my own inclinations and lived the life of a thief.”
Now, in this city of Kāśī, having been caught in the act of stealing in the house of a certain preeminent nobleman, I was bound and condemned to death.

While I was about to be executed, a rogue elephant named Mṛtyuvijaya, who delighted in violence, charged at me with his trunk curled like a staff, its bells ringing twice as loud as the cries of the people, at the command of the chief minister named Kāmapāla, who stood upon the upper terrace of the royal gate watching.

Having rushed forward, I rebuked him fearlessly; he, who had entered the hollow of a ripening *mandāra* fruit with both his staff-like arms joined together as a defensive shield, turned back as if terrified.
Again, with eyes full of fury, I brought him face to face with exceedingly cruel goads of speech and blows of my feet.
He too, his anger redoubled, having been rebuked and struck by me, turned back and fled.

Then, having approached him impetuously, I provoked the driver to anger; and he, enraged, shouting, "Ah, you are dead, you wretched elephant!", repeatedly struck his own elephant with a sharp goad and somehow turned it toward me at the side of the gateway.
Then I said: "Let this two-legged insect depart!"
"Let some other leader of the elephants be brought here,
so that I, having sported for a moment, may go to my destined destination.
As soon as he saw me roaring in anger, the driver, disregarding his harsh commands, fled.
The minister summoned me again and said, "Good sir,
this is indeed Death himself, named Mṛtyuvijaya, who delights in violence. Even he has been reduced to such a state by you."
"Therefore, desist from this defiled action; why do you not resolve to conduct yourself toward us with noble behavior?
"As you have commanded," he replied, and being thus addressed by me, he behaved toward me like a friend.

And once, when I questioned him in private and confidence had been established between us, he related his own life story: "In Kusumapura, there was a minister of King Ripuñjaya named Dharmapāla, whose wisdom was renowned and who was a sage learned in the scriptures."
This man’s son, named Sumitra, is equal to his father in the qualities of wisdom. I am his younger half-brother.
While I was sporting among the courtesans, he, who delights in discipline, restrained me.
Having escaped from my unavoidable misfortune and wandering at will through various directions, I arrived here in this pleasure grove of Vāraṇasī. There,
having gone out with her companions to worship Madanadamana, I fell in love with the daughter of Caṇḍasiṃha, the lord of Kāśī, named Kāntimatī, as she was playing with a ball.
By some means I was able to meet her; then, while living in concealment within the princess's quarters, she became pregnant by me and gave birth to a son.
Thinking him "born dead," he was abandoned on a pleasure-mountain by his attendants out of fear that their secret would be revealed; and the Śabara woman, fearing the cremation ground, took him away.
While she was returning at midnight, she was seized by royal guards patrolling for criminals; threatened and terrified of a harsh punishment, she disclosed almost all of the secret.

By the king’s command, while I was sleeping trustfully in a mountain cave at midnight, she pointed me out; I was bound with ropes as they were available, led to the cremation ground, and sought to be slain by a sword raised by a Mātaṅga. By the power of destiny, my bonds were severed;
I snatched that sword away, struck that outcaste and several others, and escaped.
Wandering helplessly through the forest, I was once approached by a maiden of celestial form, accompanied by her attendants, her face bathed in tears.

Bowing with her head— its hair tossing about her face and its sprout-like hands folded in *añjali*— she sat with me in the cool shade of a certain great banyan tree and asked, "Who are you, dear lady?"
"From where have you come, and for what reason do you show favor toward me?"— thus addressed by me with longing, she rained down a shower of honey-like words: "Noble sir,
I am the daughter of Maṇibhadra, the lord of the Yakṣas, named Tārāvalī."
Once, while returning after paying my respects to Lopāmudrā, the wife of Agastya, I saw a certain boy weeping in Vārāṇasī, the abode of the departed on Mount Malaya.
Out of intense affection, I took him and brought him into the presence of my parents;
and my father brought him into the assembly hall of the god Āḷakeśvara.
Then, having been summoned, I was questioned by the friend of Hara:
"Child, child, what is your feeling toward this boy?
I replied, "I have affection for this child as if he were my own son. He remarked, "The poor girl speaks the truth," and proceeded to tell a very long story based on that.
In this matter, this much has been understood by me: "You, it is said, are Śaunaka, Śūdraka, and Kāmapāla, who are not distinct;
Bandhumatī, Vinayavatī, and Kāntimatī are not distinct;
and Vedimatī, Āryadāsī, and Somadevī are likewise one and the same."
I was Haṃsāvalī, Śūrasenā, Sulocanā, and Ananyā;
