Then, while I was gladdened by the friction of passion unleashed by the unrestrained play of thousands of women gathered for continuous song and music, and entirely dependent on my thirst for sensual pleasure, King Jayasiṃha of Andhra suddenly arrived at that vulnerable moment with a vast army brought for the purpose of crossing the waters and seized me along with my wife. My beloved Kanakalekhā, her eyes trembling with fear, was led away together with her circle of female companions.

Then, my thoughts of food eclipsed by the burning pain produced by the fire of love, and with the luster of my body faded as I brooded upon my beloved, I reflected thus: "That daughter of the King of Kaliṅga has fallen into the hands of the enemy along with her father and mother;
that king, his fortitude cast aside, will surely seek to seize her."
"And if she were unable to endure it, that virtuous woman would perish instantly by means of poison, aconite, or the like.
And when she has reached such a state, the maintenance of the body of this person [the husband] would be destroyed by no other cause.
What would his destiny be? Thus he spoke.
In the meantime, an elder brother arriving from the city of Āndhra was seen;
he related this story: "It seems that Jayasiṃha, though intent on killing Kardana due to the rivalry arising from the many insults he had endured, spared him because of his passion for Kanakalekhā;
and that maiden, being possessed by a certain yakṣa, does not stand before any other man."
"The king exerts himself by gathering a caravan of men with the intent of repelling him, yet there is no success.

Encouraged by this, I went to the site of Śaṅkara’s dance arena, pulled out a mass of matted hair from the hollow of the neck of an old *sāla* tree, and assuming the state of a matted-haired ascetic, covered my entire body with a collection of rags and bark garments, and took on several disciples.
I observed those people, who were constantly joyful because they were drawn from the populace by various wonderful performances and by the distribution of food and clothing;
and after some days, I arrived at the city of Āndhra.
Not far from it was a lake resembling a mass of water, variegated with fragments of filaments fallen from clusters of lotus petals torn by flocks of *kalahaṃsa* swans.

Having made his dwelling in the forest on the shore of that lake, which was crowned by rows of cranes, he remained there, skilled in deceiving all the townspeople by means of the various wondrous feats described by his disciples.

Thus did people proclaim his ill-fame in every direction: “This ascetic, who sleeps upon the bare ground on the shore of a lake in this aged wilderness, is said to have all the Vedas, along with their secret Upanishads and six auxiliary branches, present at the tip of his tongue.”
Regarding other treatises that he does not know, he will determine their meaning from those who do;
his face is never stained by falsehood.
And this mass of compassion is still embodied.
By his gathering [of disciples] today, my initiation has finally achieved its purpose after a long time.
For by scattering even a few particles of the dust from his feet upon one's head, many a chronic ailment—long uncurable by physicians—is instantly removed for many people.
"By the sprinkling of the water used for washing his feet, the fierce planetary influences that transgress the control of all kings vanish in a single instant from those whose heads are stainless;
yet, it is impossible to know the limit of his power,
nor is there even a grain of egoism in him."

This story, circulating from the mouths of many people, was able to attract that Kṣatriya, whose mind was intensely devoted to the act of repelling the servants of Kubera—the presiding deity of Kanakalekhā. Coming day after day with the greatest respect and honoring him, he gathered disciples by means of wealth;
and having found his opportunity, he once requested him slowly for the accomplishment of his desired object.
Steadfast in meditation and possessing the treasury of knowledge that perceives the true state of things, I gazed upon him, scrutinized him, and said: "Father, this effort is indeed well-placed;

for the attainment of that jewel of a maiden—who is a singular mass of all auspicious marks—is the very means for winning the Lady Earth herself, who is adorned by the girdle of the Milk Ocean and graced by the pearl necklace of the thousands of rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā."
"And that Yakṣa who presides over it does not allow any king to behold her, whose eyes are like a playful, curved blue lotus; therefore,
let this be endured for three days, during which time I shall strive to accomplish this purpose."
When the king had thus been instructed and had departed, I went forth at night— when the moon’s rays were absent and the ten directions were swallowed by a mass of dense darkness,

and when the eyes of all people were fettered by sleep— to that bank of the lake which was secluded from holy places; there, with a certain digging tool, I laboriously made a gap in the dense ground that lay submerged beneath the water's surface.
Having determined that the shore was free from suspicion by people— its openings and crevices covered with thick stones and bricks—
and having purified his body with a bath at the beginning of the day, he [became] like a jewel fastened to the tip of a pearl necklace formed by a continuous string of stars;
a true lion capable of alone tearing apart the scent-elephant of the darkness of night.
A dancer in the graceful performance of the dance upon the peaks of the golden mountain,
a sole crocodile leaping over the rows of thick waves in the ocean of the sky,
and the witness to what ought and ought not to be done.
Having worshipped Sahasrārcis with handfuls of red lotuses— his mass of rays acting as the cosmetic ointment for the limbs of the women who are the quarters of the sky— I retired to my own dwelling.
And when three days had passed,

When the lord of the day— resplendent like a jar-like breast anointed with red sandalwood paste belonging to the lady Twilight, who had been united with the body of Śaṅkara known as the Sky (the firmament) after her tormenting of the Daughter of the Mountain King, and whose hue was common to the slopes of red chalk on the peak of the Setting Mountain—
the lord of men arrived; his crown covered by the rays from the nails of his feet placed upon the earth, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
And he was instructed: "By good fortune, the attainment of your desired goal has been seen!
For in this world, the goddesses of prosperity do not resort to an embodied being who is devoid of effort;
and all auspicious things are ever-present in the hands of those who are untiring."

Since this lake has been consecrated by these people— whose minds have been drawn by your most excellent conduct, which is stainless, honored, and performed with great devotion— it is such that your success shall be achieved here today.
Therefore, it must be entered for bathing tonight when the night has reached its midpoint.
Immediately after entering, one should seize those creatures that move constantly and wander within the depths of the water and rest as much as possible.

Then, for a person whose ears are attuned to the sound of a royal swan— its body pierced by the tips of the quivering stalks of lotus clusters submerged by water splashing against the bank— the tumultuous clamor of the mass of water will suddenly become audible.

And when the sound of the water has subsided there, with his limbs moistened and his gaze slightly reddened, in whatever form he emerges— having observed that form which brings delight to the eyes of all people— the Yakṣa will not be able to stand before him. Furthermore, the maiden’s heart, fettered by the chains of a firmly established affection, would in a single moment become an unbearable obstacle to any other sight.

And for this lady of the earth, one should contemplate the discus held in the palm of her hand— which has not merely disregarded but utterly destroyed the circle of her enemies— of this there is no doubt.
If you so desire, let hundreds of net-spreaders be summoned and, after consulting with authorized officials of firm intellect learned in many sciences and with other groups of well-wishers,
let a lake be constructed with its interior visible at will by hundreds of inner-court men.
"And the protection within a radius of thirty *daṇḍas* from the bank must be diligently maintained by the soldiers;
for who knows what the enemies might attempt through some vulnerability there?
This struck at the very core of his heart.

The officials in charge of that matter, unable to find any flaw in the situation and having ascertained that the King’s desire—born of his intense passion for the maiden—was utterly steadfast, did not prohibit this course of action.
While he remained thus, with a firm resolve to attain her, he was addressed: “O King, you have stood here in the presence of these people for a long time.”
"Nor is staying long in one place recommended for us.
Furthermore, once you have accomplished your purpose here, you will not see me again.
Since you have obtained food and other necessities within your kingdom, if you do not perform some service for him, your destination will be censured by the noble."
In this regard, this is the cause for its long duration,
and that has now been established.
Go home.

"Having bathed with water appropriate to the occasion and with heart-pleasing perfumes, wearing white garlands and unguents, and having propitiated the hosts of *taitilas* upon the earth's surface with gifts suited to your power, you should strive for the attainment of your goal—having dispelled the mass of nocturnal darkness with thousands of flames from wicks made of cotton threads steeped in sesame oil and fastened to the tips of rods.
He, indeed, displaying his gratitude, said: "This failure is itself success; for..."
That the Noble Ones are absent here is a hardship;
and this lack of attachment is cruel, for it causes one to abandon a servant who has committed no offense.
"And the words of the great should not be disregarded. Having said this, he went to his house to bathe.

I, having departed, remained at the edge of the lake in a secluded spot during the dead of night, hidden within a hollow and listening intently through a slight opening. When midnight had arrived, the king—having performed the rites as instructed, having stationed guards in various places, and having summoned the fishermen—plunged with playful grace into the waters of the lake, which were now free of internal thorns and devoid of suspicion.

Having gone to the bottom of the lake, I seized that elephant— whose hair was disheveled and whose ears and trunk were drawn together— as it lay there in the manner of a crocodile, hidden from its enemies; with merciless blows of my hands and feet, as fierce as the striking of a harsh rod of Time, I brought it to its end in a single moment,
and then, dragging its body and placing it within a hollow, I emerged from the water.
And it was a source of great wonder to the assembled soldiers to behold that change of appearance.

Mounted upon the neck of an elephant, adorned with all the royal insignia such as the white parasol, and proceeding along the royal highway—which had been cleared of people out of fear of being struck by the staffs of the most fierce rod-bearers—I spent that night without any pleasure in sleep, my eyes fixed in rapture. And when the solar disc—resembling the head of a rutting elephant smeared with lac-dye, and serving as a jeweled mirror for the celestial maiden of the eastern quarter—was brought within the range of the people's eyes;

Having accomplished what was to be done, seated upon a royal throne resplendent with rows of jewels formidable with their lattice of rays, I addressed my companions—who were sitting nearby, their limbs constrained by apprehension as they observed my conduct according to custom: "Behold the power of the Sage! For by the stainless refinement of that unconquerable ascetic, there has appeared in this lake—which abounds in the presence of lotuses and is filled with joyful swarms of bees—a form of even greater beauty, whose luster resembles the petals of a lotus."
Success has been achieved!
Today, the heads of all nihilists shall be bowed down in shame.
Therefore, let the abodes of the lords of the gods—Śiva, Yama, Brahmā, and the others—now be honored with dances, songs, and worship performed with devotion.
"Let wealth that is capable of dispelling the afflictions of the multitude of supplicants be brought forth from the palace and elsewhere," he said.

With their eyes wide with joy at the singular delight of this wondrous sentiment, they repeatedly offered blessings, saying, "Victory, O Lord of the World! Victory, as you surpassingly shroud the ten directions with your own glory, eclipsing the fame of the primordial kings! Thus they performed the duties as instructed.

And once, when Śaśāṅkasenā—a maiden who was the very heart of my beloved and her confidante—had come to me on some other business, I spoke to her in secret: "Has this person ever been seen by you before? Then, with a heart reaching the height of joy, she slightly revealed the creeper-like luster of her teeth while moving them with playful languor; her sprout-like lips were partially concealed by her gracefully curved fingers.
With her eyes— unadorned and trembling from being moistened by tears of joy—
she joined her palms in reverence and said, "I know full well that this cannot be some kind of illusion created by a magician;
for how else could this be?"
"Speak," she said slowly,
with an unrestrained affection; and I, having related everything to her, produced in my companion an unsurpassed joy of heart by means of the message transmitted through her mouth.

"Furthermore, through an alliance freely granted and most honorably bestowed by the Lord of Kaliṅga—who was won over by this beloved lady—he has been ruling the kingdoms of both Andhra and Kaliṅga. Desiring to invade him, that enemy of yours sent [the King of Aṅga] with a small force to assist the King of Aṅga, who was about to be attacked.
Having arrived here, his mind was overwhelmed by a flood of joy from the chance meeting with you and your circle of friends."
His friends, their lips bathed in the moonlight of his smile, congratulated him on that skill and said: "Wondrous indeed is this conduct of the Great Sage!
Truly, even most arduous asceticism bears fruit here. Let the jest rest for now;
we have seen here the true nature of wisdom and courage, which touch upon the highest excellence of joy. Thus they spoke.
Again, saying, "May you descend," King Rājavāhana cast upon the renowned man of great learning a glance like a blooming lotus.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Adventures of Mantragupta," in *The Deeds of the Ten Princes* (*Daśakumāracarita*) composed by the illustrious Daṇḍin. **Chapter Eight**

Then he too related: "Your Majesty, while wandering through the Vindhya forest, I saw a certain young boy, about eight years old, who was undeserving of suffering yet tormented by hunger and thirst near a certain well.
And he spoke with a voice trembling from fear: 'O noble one, [I am lost! "
"Noble sir, please grant me your assistance.
To counteract this life-threatening thirst of mine, someone who is my sole refuge has fallen here into this well while drawing up water."
Thinking, "I am not able to rescue that man from the *tamāla* tree," I then approached, rescued the old man by means of some creeping vine,

and restored life to that boy by providing him with water drawn from the mouth of a bamboo tube and five fruits of the *lakucha* tree— which had been raised on a bamboo pole and then felled with stones from its summit.
Sitting at the foot of a tree, I said to that old man: "Father, who is this boy,
and who are you?"
"And how has she fallen into this calamity? he asked.

With a voice choked with tears, he replied: "Listen, O noble one! There is a country named Vidarbha. In it dwells [my brother], an ornament of the Bhoja lineage, like an incarnation of Dharma himself."
An exceedingly virtuous being,
truthful in speech, and generous.
He was disciplined, a leader of his subjects,
and one who had won over his servants.
Possessing fame, exalted,
and characterized by industriousness through both intelligence and physical form.
He takes the scriptures as his authority; he undertakes what is possible, appropriate, and feasible; he honors the wise and exalts his servants.
One who exalts his kinsmen,
humbles his enemies,
and does not lend an ear to incoherent prattle.
Never once satiated with virtues,
exceedingly proficient in the arts, and most intimate with the compendiums on dharma and artha.
He was exceedingly grateful even for the slightest good deed; he supervised both the treasury and the transport of goods; and he diligently examined all the superintendents.
Skilled in the application of the sixfold policy, a leader of the four castes according to the path of Manu, there was a king named Puṇyavarmā, who possessed auspicious fame.
Having lived out a full human lifespan through meritorious deeds, he was subsequently born among the gods by means of non-meritorious karma.
Immediately after that, one named Anantavarman, his successor, ruled over the earth.
Although he was endowed with every virtue, by the turn of fate, he did not receive great respect in the administration of justice.

One day, an elderly minister named Vasurakṣita—highly esteemed by his father and possessed of bold speech—addressed him in private: “My son, it is observed that all your personal excellences, beginning from your noble lineage, appear to be entirely without deficiency.”

Your intellect is naturally acute; it has attained great proficiency in the various arts such as dance and song, as well as in painting and extensive poetic compositions, and thus excels that of others.
Nevertheless, it has not yet acquired refinement regarding the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*).
The nature of gold does not shine brightly unless purified by fire;
for a king who lacks intelligence, even if he be exceedingly exalted, does not perceive himself being climbed upon by others.
Moreover, he is unable to act by distinguishing between what is to be accomplished and the means for its accomplishment.

Furthermore, one who acts improperly and is obstructed in his duties is despised by both his own people and others. And the command of one who is held in contempt lacks the power to secure the welfare and prosperity of his subjects.

When subjects transgress the royal edict, speaking whatever they please and behaving however they wish, they will throw all established orders into confusion. And the world, becoming lawless, will [fall away] from this world and the next, [bringing ruin] upon its lord and itself.
And one would cause [the world] to fall away.
Indeed, the course of worldly life proceeds easily by means of the path seen through the lamp of scripture;
for that which is called "scripture" possesses unimpeded function regarding objects that are past, present, and future, as well as those that are concealed or remote, just like the divine eye.

"Therefore, even though you possess long and wide eyes, you are effectively blind regarding the perception of true goals due to your incapacity; hence, casting aside attachment to external sciences, master the science of polity (*daṇḍanīti*), which is the traditional lore of your lineage.
By the successful application of its principles, having attained power and perfection, and with your commands unimpeded, rule for a long time this earth girdled by the ocean.
Having heard this, [the prince replied], "The instruction given by my teachers is indeed appropriate."
"So shall it be done," he said, and entered the inner apartments.

Having overheard that news— which the king had mentioned in passing in the presence of his women— a man sat nearby who was skilled in following the king's moods, whose wealth was his favor, who was not inferior in song, dance, and instrumental music, devoted to noble women, clever with a restrained face, and expert in many modes of expression.

Vihārabhadra, an attendant of the prince who was devoted to seeking out the vital secrets of others, a mocker, one who delighted in scandal, an expert in backbiting, a taker of bribes even from the circle of ministers, a teacher of all forms of misconduct, and a helmsman of the science of erotics, addressed him with a smile: "Your Majesty,
if by the grace of fate someone becomes a worthy vessel for prosperity,"
Deceiving him with various sudden enticements, they accomplish their own ends by binding his head with ropes, covering it with a deerskin, and so forth.
Having smeared him with fresh butter and laid him down to fast,
they will seize all his possessions.
Even more terrible than they are the heretics, who would even cause one to abandon son, wife, body, and life;

if some person of sharp intellect should not wish to give up what is in his hand for the sake of this mirage, others surround him and say: “We could turn even a single *kākiṇī* into a hundred thousand *kārṣāpaṇas*;”
"We would cause all enemies to be slain without the use of weapons; we would even make a mortal man, though possessing but a single body, a universal monarch,
provided he conducts himself according to the path prescribed by us."
He, in turn, asks them: "What is that path?
They reply again: "Are they not the four royal sciences: the triple Veda (*trayī*), economics (*vārtā*), metaphysics (*anvīkṣikī*), and the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*)?
Among these, three—the triple Veda, economics, and metaphysics—are great [in scope] yet yield meager fruits."
Let those matters rest for now;
first study the *Arthaśāstra*.
This has now been condensed by the teacher Viṣṇugupta into six thousand verses for the sake of the Maurya king.
"This very [Veda], when studied and properly performed, is capable of accomplishing the actions as described.
He studies it, saying "So be it," and he listens to it.
One reaches old age right there;
for that treatise, it is said, is connected to other treatises,
and without knowing the entirety of the body of literature, one will not truly comprehend it.
Let it be that the realization of that goal occurs after much or little time;
however, by one who has mastered the treatise, even his wife and children must not be trusted from the very beginning.
Even for the sake of filling his own belly, he knows exactly how much rice yields how much cooked food.
One should give [the food] according to measure and weight, thinking, "This much fuel is sufficient to cook this much rice.

And when the king has risen, having placed his fistful or half-fistful [of food] inside his mouth—whether his mouth has been washed or not—he should hear the entire account of income and expenditure during the first or eighth part of the day.

While he is listening, those fraudulent officials steal twice as much from him; and those forty methods of embezzlement taught by Akṣapāda, they will devise a thousand variations upon with their own intellects alone.

In the second [hell], one lives in misery with ears burning from the abuse of people who are quarreling with one another; there, judges and others, awarding victory and defeat according to their own whims, yoke their master and themselves with sin and infamy, yet they obtain the opportunity to bathe. In the third [hell], one obtains the opportunity to bathe.
As long as the food he has eaten remains undigested, his fear of the poison does not subside at all.
In the fourth watch, he rises while still stretching out his hand to seize gold.
In the fifth, he undergoes great exhaustion from contemplating spells.

Even there, the ministers, acting like mediators among themselves, join together in secret to arbitrarily distort faults and virtues, the reports of envoys and spies, feasibility and impossibility, and the circumstances of place, time, and action; thus they live off their own and their friends' circles.
Having secretly incited internal and external dissensions, they then appear to pacify them openly, thereby seizing control of the master who has been rendered powerless.
In the sixth [week], one should either engage in wandering at will or practice mantra recitation.
Thus, this is the extent of his time for unrestrained wandering, during which three channels increased by three-quarters [of a unit] pass;
in the seventh, there is the exertion of inspecting the fourfold army;
and in the eighth, for him who is a companion to the commander-in-chief, there is the distress of contemplating valor.
Having again performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*),
during the first part of the night, secret agents (*gūḍhapuruṣa*) are to be seen;
and through their agency, extremely cruel operations involving weapons, fire, and poison are to be carried out.
In the second watch, immediately after eating, he should begin his private Vedic recitation like a *śrotriya*.
In the third, he should lie down to the sound of musical instruments; it is said that he should sleep during the fourth and fifth watches as well.
But how could the pleasure of sleep come to this wretched man, whose mind is overwhelmed by the constant toil of anxious reflection?
Furthermore, in the sixth [chapter], there is the undertaking of reflection on the treatises and reflection on duties;

in the seventh, however, there is the receiving of mantras and the dispatching of messengers. And these messengers increase their wealth through trade on a path free from tolls and obstacles, having obtained goods by means of pleasant speech in both places regarding names.
Even though the task is non-existent, they wander incessantly, having produced it slightly through ignorance.
On the eighth day, the domestic priests and others approach him and say: "Today an evil dream was seen; the planets are ill-placed, and the omens are inauspicious."
Let propitiatory rites be performed;
let every implement for the oblation be made of gold alone.
This being so, the ritual action becomes meritorious.
These Brāhmaṇas are equal to Brahmā;
the auspicious rites performed by them become most excellent.
They are difficult to approach, have many offspring, are performers of sacrifices, and are full of vigor, yet even now they do not accept gifts.

"Furthermore, what is given to them leads to heaven, long life, and the destruction of misfortune. Having thus caused much and more to be given, they themselves consume it secretly through those intermediaries. Thus, for one who does not know the path of policy (*anayajña*) and spends day and night in such a manner—devoid of even a fraction of prescribed happiness, abounding in toil, and characterized by incessant harassment—let alone universal sovereignty (*cakravartitā*), even his own small domain would be difficult to protect.
For that which he gives, authorized by those learned in the scriptures (*śāstrajña*), [is truly effective].
That he honors me and speaks kindly to me— all this is merely to deceive me; thus, there is no trust.

For lack of trust is the birthplace of misfortune. To the extent that a certain course of conduct is necessary for the maintenance of worldly life, that is already established by common experience; there is no need for a treatise on this matter.
For even an infant seeks to obtain the breast-milk from its mother through various means; therefore, setting aside excessive restraint, let these things be experienced.
They enjoy the pleasures of the senses as they please; yet others teach: "The sense-faculties must be conquered in this way, and the group of six internal enemies must be abandoned in this way."
"The group of means beginning with conciliation (sāma) should be employed incessantly toward both one's own people and others;
time should be spent solely in deliberating upon peace and war, and not even the slightest opportunity for ease should be granted."
Even by these crows of ministers, the wealth acquired through theft from you is enjoyed only within the houses of slave-girls;
and who are these wretches?
As for those authors of Tantras who are harsh in their incantations—Śukra, Aṅgiras, Viśālākṣa, Bāhudantīputra, Parāśara, and others—was the group of six internal enemies conquered by them?
Or perhaps they have carried out the practice of the scriptures;
for even among them, success and failure are seen regarding the tasks they have undertaken,
and many who are reciting are outshone by those who do not recite at all.
Is this not indeed appropriate for Your Majesty:
that your birth is worthy of homage by the entire world,
and your youth is fresh and unimpaired?
Your bodies are beautiful and your prosperity is immeasurable;

yet, O trees, do not let all of that be ruined by the sowing of mantras— a practice which causes universal distrust, obstructs the enjoyment of happiness, and, through its manifold conceptualizations, leaves one in constant doubt regarding every undertaking.
For you possess ten thousand elephants, three hundred thousand horses, and an infinite host of infantry.
Moreover, the treasuries are already filled with gold and jewels;

even if this entire world of living beings were to consume them all for a full thousand ages, it would not exhaust your storehouses. Why then is this effort expended to acquire wealth through unjust means when it is already so abundant?
For life, indeed, for those who are born, consists of only four or five days;
even within that, the portion of time suitable for enjoyment is exceedingly small. Yet the unwise perish while they are still in the very act of acquiring it.
"They do not desire to taste even a fraction of wealth that has been acquired.

What more need be said? Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to your devoted inner circle who are capable of bearing it, enjoy yourself with the women of the harem who resemble celestial nymphs; and by engaging in assemblies for song, music, and wine as the seasons permit, make your life fruitful in a fitting manner. Thus he spoke, and touching the ground with his five limbs, his crest kissing his folded palms, he lay there for a long time.
And the women of the inner apartments laughed, their eyes blossoming with joy;
and the Lord of Men said with a smile, "Arise! Surely you are gurus because of your beneficial instruction."
"Why have you performed something so contrary to my weighty command? Having said this, he raised him up and remained with an abundance of playful jesting.

Then, during these days, though repeatedly urged by the elder minister regarding the matter at hand, he promised verbally but disregarded him in his mind alone, treating him as one who does not understand his thoughts.
Then this thought occurred to the minister: “Alas! How foolish I have been out of delusion!
By urging him toward something he finds distasteful, I have become like an unwanted guest to him and an object of his ridicule;
it is evident that his behavior has changed from its former state.”
For instance:
he does not look at me with affection, nor does he speak with a smile.
He does not reveal secrets,
he does not touch her hand,
and he does not show compassion in times of distress.
He does not favor everyone indiscriminately, he does not send gifts for the sake of seduction,
and he does not boast of his own good deeds.
He does not inquire after my household affairs, he does not look toward my partisans, and he does not include me among those consulted in matters close to his heart.
He does not allow me to enter the inner apartments; moreover, he appoints me to tasks for which I am unfit, and he permits my seat to be occupied by others.
He displays confidence toward my enemies, he does not provide an answer to what I have said, and he censures those who possess faults equal to my own.
He mocks me at my very vitals,
rejects even my own views as they are being described by me,
and takes no pleasure in the precious objects sent by me.
He proclaims the lapses of those who know the way in my presence before fools;
as Cāṇakya truly said: "Calamities that follow one's thoughts may become dear, while even gifts, if they exclude one from their true nature, would become objects of hatred."
Nevertheless, what recourse is there?
This sovereign, though undisciplined, must not be abandoned by those like us who follow the path of their fathers and grandfathers.
Yet, even while not abandoning him, what service can we perform when our words are not heard?
In every respect, this kingdom has fallen into the hands of Vasantabhanu, the King of Ashmaka, who is skilled in policy.
Might the calamities that are to come bring him back to his natural state?
For even if some resentment were to arise toward him regarding matters of misfortune where blame is easily found, it might yet cause him to take pleasure in virtuous conduct.
"Let it be that some misfortune will surely come to pass;
yet, with the tongues of the slanderers paralyzed, I shall somehow remain in my position without falling from it.
Thus it was when the minister had departed.
And while the king was acting according to his own desires,
there was one named Candrapālita, the son of Indrapālita, the minister of the chief of horses;
having become known as one of evil conduct, he was banished by his father.

Surrounded by many throngs of *cāraṇas*, numerous female artisans of no small skill, and many disguised servants, he approached and brought Vihārabhadra under his control through various diversions; and by this very means, he gained a foothold among the royalty. Having found his opportunity, whatever vice the king undertook, he described it as being exactly so: "Your Majesty,..."
For hunting is indeed beneficial in a way that nothing else is;
for here, through the excellence of physical exertion, one becomes a helper in times of calamity, possessing the speed of the legs capable of traversing long distances,
and through the reduction of phlegm, one gains the kindling of the digestive fire, which is the sole root of health.
From the reduction of fat, there arise stability, firmness, and extreme lightness of the limbs;
endurance of cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, and thirst;
and knowledge of the mental activities of living beings in their various states.
The prevention of crop damage through the killing of deer, gavayas, and other such animals; the clearing of obstacles from land routes by the slaying of wolves, tigers, and the like;
and the inspection of mountainous and forest regions suitable for various types of labor.
There are many virtues: winning the confidence of forest tribes, and intimidating the enemy by kindling the power of their enthusiasm;
even in gambling, there is incomparable magnanimity of intent from the relinquishing of a heap of wealth as if it were mere straw.
Because victory and defeat are unstable, there is no certainty regarding joy or dispute;
there is an increase in indignation caused solely by human effort;
and there is infinite intellectual skill in detecting fraudulent practices—such as those involving dice, hands, or the ground—which are extremely difficult to perceive.

From the withdrawal of the mind to a single object, there arises an exceedingly wonderful one-pointedness; an extreme delight in daring acts accompanied by resolute determination; and, through association with extremely harsh men, an invincibility against others.
It consists of maintaining one's pride and sustaining the body without meanness;
even while enjoying the company of excellent women, it involves making one's wealth and religious duties bear fruit.
Puṣkala possessed self-confidence befitting a man, skill in discerning the inner state of others, conduct untainted by greed,
and proficiency in all the arts.

Skill in both intellect and speech through the constant employment of expedients in matters such as acquiring what has not been obtained, guarding what has been acquired, protecting what has been guarded, enjoying what has been protected, reflecting upon what has been enjoyed, and conciliating those who are angry;
being worthy of public esteem due to an excellent refinement of the body and an auspicious appearance;
and being supremely beloved by friends.
Great regard for one's attendants, the habit of speaking with a smile, and an abundance of noble character.
It involves following courtesy and ensuring the welfare of both worlds through the procreation of offspring. Furthermore,
even regarding drinking, it consists in establishing a desirable stage of life by consuming various fermented liquors (*āsava*) that are highly effective at dispelling diverse passions.
Through the excellence of egoity, there is the suppression of all suffering;
through the kindling of passion born of the limbs, there is the fanning of the power for the enjoyment of women;
and through the wiping away of offenses, there is the extraction of the thorn from the mind.
It kindled the passion born of the limbs, inflamed the power of enjoyment with women,
removed the thorn from the mind by wiping away offenses,
and increased confidence through unrestrained chatter that revealed what should not be heard.
The state of being solely intent on bliss due to the absence of attachment to envy;
the continuous experience of the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest;
and the gathering together of one's circle of friends through a disposition toward sharing.
Its auspicious beauty is incomparable, its splendors are unsurpassed, and it possesses the quality of being martial because it removes fear and suffering.
"Harshness of speech, severe punishment, and the embezzlement of wealth— these are indeed the means for providing assistance as the occasion demands.
For a king who delights in tranquility like a sage is not capable of overcoming a hostile faction,
nor is he able to uphold the governance of the world."
He, too, followed his master’s counsel with extreme devotion, as if it were the instruction of a guru;
and the subjects, conforming to his character, indulged in vices without restraint. And because everyone shared the same faults, no one exerted himself to seek out another's weaknesses.
The superintendents of the departments, whose nature was identical to that of their master, consumed the fruits of their own labors;
consequently, the channels of income gradually crumbled away,
while the outlets for expenditure increased day by day through the influence of parasites over the sovereign.

The leading men among the vassals, city-dwellers, and country-folk, having gained the king’s confidence through their shared character, were admitted by him into drinking parties along with his kinsmen; there they practiced their respective customs and excesses.

And in the Aṅga territories, the king misconducted himself under various pretexts. Furthermore, within the harems of those whose conduct had become corrupted, these men lived with little fear and much pleasure.

And all the women of good family, delighting in speech full of easy seductive wiles and having broken the restraints of virtuous conduct, did not value their husbands even as much as a blade of grass, nor did they heed the counsels of their brothers-in-law;
and from that root, quarrels arose among those filled with resentment,
and the weak were slain by the strong.
The wealth of the wealthy was plundered by thieves and others;
their dignity was stolen away, and the paths of sin were trodden upon.
With their kinsmen slain and their riches seized, and tormented by execution and imprisonment, the subjects, with throats choked with tears, wailed aloud with unrestrained voices.
Punishment, when administered unjustly, gave rise to fear and anger;
greed took root among impoverished families; and those of high spirit, being insulted, were consumed by indignation;
and incitements to hostility spread toward various improper acts.

And at that time, by describing the abundance of game and the hunting attire, he lured them into mountain valleys with narrow, trackless paths filled with dry grass, bamboo, and thickets, where he set fires from the entrances;

by encouraging the slaughter of tigers and other beasts, he caused them to fall into their mouths; and by creating the thirst of a mirage at desired wells, he led those who had wandered too far to their death through the intensification of hunger and thirst.
By rushing along uneven paths due to hidden thorns, shrubs, precipices, and chasms;

by the drawing out of thorns from their feet with poison-tipped knives; by being made solitary through the scattering and dispersal of their followers in all directions, leading to their slaughter at will;
and by the discharge of arrows at those who had offended them under the guise of deer—[they were destroyed].

By mounting mountain peaks difficult to ascend under the pretext of a wager, with descents unobserved by others; by obstructing small detachments of soldiers in the forests under the guise of forest-dwellers;
and by forceful infiltrations during crowds gathered for dice games, bird-fights, expeditions, festivals, and the like.

For others, [one should act] by instigating violence; by making public the unpleasant things derived from secret and fabricated offenses after having them proven before witnesses, using heroic deeds as a means to protect one's reputation; and by inciting paramours toward the wives of others under the guise of friendship, or by attacking husbands and then presenting those acts as crimes of violence.
By luring suitable women into secret trysts and then attacking them from behind with unspeakable means of execution;

by enticing them into entering caves, digging for treasure, or performing mantra-rites, and then killing them under the pretext of obstacles; and by sending them to ride intoxicated elephants and then causing their downfall through accidents.
By causing wild elephants to be provoked and then withdrawing from the circles of noble men who had been targeted;
by delighting suitable women day and night and thereby inducing consumption;
and by his skill in the preparation of aesthetic flavors regarding garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents.

By means of medical treatments, other methods for aggravating the disease, and various other stratagems employed by the King of Aśmaka, the sharp rasadās and others caused Anantavarman’s camp—its foremost heroes having been eliminated—to fall into a state of ruin. Then Vasantabhānu incited Bhānuvarman, the king of Vanavāsī, to wage war against Anantavarman. Having his kingdom’s borders invaded by him, Anantavarman mobilized his forces to launch an attack against him.
The lord of Aśmaka, having approached earlier than all his vassals, became his most beloved;
the other vassals also associated with him,
and having gone near, they settled on the bank of the Narmadā.
At that time, Antavarman summoned the actress of the great feudatory Kuntalapati Avantideva, named Kṣmātalorvaśī, who was highly praised for her skill in dancing by Candrapālita and others,
and watched her dance; being deeply enamored, he then enjoyed her when she was intoxicated with wine.
The King of Aśmaka, however, addressed the Lord of Kuntala in private: “This king is intoxicated; he violates our wives.
How much more can this contempt be endured?
I have a hundred elephants.”
"And those five hundred [men]—
then we two, having consulted together, shall instigate Muralēśa, Vīrasēna, Ṛcīkēśa, Ekavīra, Koṅkaṇapati, Kumāragupta, Sāsikyanātha, and Nāgapāla.
They, being unable to endure his misconduct, will surely come over to our side according to our counsel."
"And this Vanavāsya is my dear friend;
we shall strike him from behind while he is preoccupied with that ill-mannered man in front,
and having divided his treasury and transport, we shall seize them."
And when he had joyfully accepted these,
[the king gave him] twenty pieces of fine silk garments and twenty-five palas of gold and saffron.
Having presented them as gifts through the mouth of a trusted messenger and consulted with those feudatories, he established them also in his own view.
On the following day, due to his hatred for policy, Anantavarman met his death at the hands of those feudatories and Vānavāsya.
Vasantabhānu, having taken possession of that depleted treasury and transport force, divided it according to their efforts and strength and took it for himself.
"By your permission, I shall be satisfied with whatever portion I receive"—saying this out of deceit, he became compliant toward everyone.
Using that very bait as a pretext, he incited a quarrel and destroyed all his vassals;
moreover, he himself seized their entire property.
Having favored Vānavāmya by granting him a certain portion [of the kingdom], he returned and brought the entire realm of Anantavarman under his own control.
In the meantime, the elder minister Vasurakṣita, having conspired with several hereditary servants, [seized] this boy Bhāskaravarman and his elder sister,
the thirteen-year-old Mañjuvādinī.
And as he was fleeing, taking with him the mother of these two, the great queen Vasundharā, he abandoned his body due to a fever born of the heat of his impending calamity.

My friends, however, having carried her to Māhiṣmatī, presented the queen along with her children to her husband’s half-brother, Mitravarmā. But that ignoble man regarded that noble lady with improper intent.
Rebuked by her with the words, "This woman of unblemished conduct desires the kingdom for her son," she, out of cruelty, sought to kill that boy.
But having learned of this, the Queen commanded me: "Dear Nālījaṅgha, [go to him]."
"O Jīva, if this child survives, place him anywhere and live;
if I too am to live, I shall follow him.
Let me know when you have set out safely on your journey."
Having rested this foot-sore traveler for several days at a certain hamlet to comfort him,
I fled along a difficult path, fearing the arrival of the king’s men.
There, wishing to give water to him who was tormented by a cruel thirst, I slipped and fell into this well, where I was rescued by you in this manner.
"Therefore, O Prince, who are without refuge, be yourself the refuge for this one," he said, joining his palms in reverence.

When I asked him, "Of what caste is his mother? he replied, "When I was thus questioned, he joined his palms in reverence and said: 'He is the son of Kusumadhanvan, the Lord of Kosala, born of Sāgaradattā, the daughter of Vaiśravaṇa, a merchant of Pāṭaliputra.'"
“My mother has been born! [he cried].
“If that is so, then this is my maternal grandfather, as well as my father’s,” I said, and with affection I embraced him.
The elder asked, “Which of Sindhudatta’s sons is your father?”
When the name "Suśruta" was uttered, he rejoiced exceedingly.

I, however, having made the vow, "Having uprooted this youth—who is arrogant due to his mother's influence—by means of the very same policy used against Aśmaka, I shall establish him in his father’s position," pondered, "How shall I satisfy his hunger?
Just then, there arrived two deer that had passed by three snares belonging to a certain hunter, along with that hunter himself.
From his hand, I snatched away the two remaining arrows and the bow, and slew him;
one arrow struck him through the feathers, while the other fell without reaching the feathers.
Having given that single deer to the hunter, I...
I removed the hair from the skin of another animal and extracted the *kloman* (lungs) and other internal organs;
having disemboweled it and cut off its limbs, feet, neck, and so forth, I roasted them on burning coals. With that meat, I satisfied the hunger of those two and of myself.
While performing this task, I asked the Kirāta, who was exceedingly delighted with my skill, "Do you know the news concerning Māhiṣmatī?"
He said: “I do not know why tiger skins and leather bags were being sold there when I arrived by chance;

however, it is said that one named Pracaṇḍavarman, the younger brother of Caṇḍavarman, is coming here desiring to marry Mañjuvādinī, the daughter of Mitravarman, and because of this, the city is in a state of great festivity.

Then, whispering into the ear of Jīrṇa, I said: “The rogue Mitravarman, having gained the confidence of his mother through proper treatment of his daughter, intends to draw the boy away through her influence and kill him.”
Having returned, you must report this favorable news and my own condition to the Queen in secret; then, you must publicly proclaim that the Prince has been devoured by a tiger.
That evil-minded man, inwardly delighted yet outwardly displaying grief, will console the Queen.
Furthermore, she must say to him through your mouth: “Because of whom I overstepped your counsel, even that child has gone to the next world through my sin.”
"But today, I am indeed one who carries out your command.
Thus addressed by her, he will receive her with affection and comply.
Furthermore, having mixed water with this great poison named Vatsanābha and soaked a garland in it, she must strike him on the chest and the face with that garland.

“Let this very sword-stroke be yours, O most wicked one, if I am a devoted wife. Then, having immersed that garland in water consecrated by this mantra, it should be given to her own daughter. But if he dies while she remains unchanged, [the truth of her devotion is proven].
"The subjects will surely follow her as long as she remains. Furthermore, a message should be sent to Pracaṇḍavarman: 'This kingdom is without a leader;
this young girl must be taken along with him.'"
Meanwhile, disguised as Kāpālikas and receiving alms from the Queen herself, we two shall dwell outside the city near the cremation ground.
Then the Queen should speak in private to the noble elders of the citizens and the trusted elder ministers: “Today, in a dream, the goddess Vindhyavāsinī has shown me favor;
on the fourth day from today, Pracaṇḍavarman will die.”
On the fifth day, at my palace situated on the bank of the Revā,
having ensured it is free of people, when the folk have departed, a certain young Brahmin shall open the door and go out with your son.
He, having protected this kingdom, will establish your infant on the throne.

"That boy was indeed set aside by me, having assumed the form of a tigress; and this dear Mañjuvādinī has been designated as the wife for that brahmin youth. "Therefore, let this great secret remain hidden among you until it comes to pass."
Now, he departed exceedingly joyful, for this purpose had been accomplished exactly as intended.
And the report spread in every direction: "Oh, the greatness of women devoted to their husbands!
For that very stroke of the sword became for him a stroke of a garland."
"It cannot be said that this act is tainted by worldly attachment;
for that very gift given to his daughter became for her a breast-ornament, not death.
Furthermore, anyone who transgresses the command of this devoted wife shall surely be reduced to ashes."

Then, seeing me and my son entering for alms in the guise of those who observe the great vows, she, her breasts flowing with milk, rose up and spoke with words overwhelmed by joy: “O Blessed One, here is my salutation with joined palms; may this helpless person be favored.
I had a certain dream; was it true or not?”
I said, "You shall see its fruit this very day.
"If that is so, then great is the good fortune of this servant-woman of yours;
indeed, that dream was a herald of her finding a protector. Having thus consoled Mañjuvādinī, who was overcome with trepidation by the passion of seeing me, I departed.
Once again, she spoke with joy in her heart: "If that be false, then this boy of yours, Bālakapālin, must be detained by me tomorrow.

I too, with a smile, my fortitude licked by a gaze impassioned and fixed upon Mañjuvādinī, said, "So be it. Having obtained alms, I summoned Nālījaṅgha and departed from there; then, as he followed me, I slowly asked him, "Where is that long-lived and famous Pracaṇḍavarman?"
He said, "The king, casting aside all suspicion that 'this kingdom is mine,' remains in the very pavilion of the royal court, attended by bards.
Having thus instructed the old man, saying, "If that is the case, stay in the garden," he had the women descend into a certain empty hut on one side of that same area;
and the prince was appointed to guard them.
Having assumed the playful attire of an actor and musician, I approached Pracaṇḍavarman and entertained him.
When the heat had become pleasant,

I withdrew those [performances] intended for the knowledge of public assemblies— namely, dancing, singing, various cries and so forth, hand-movements, walking on hands, standing on one leg, stepping on a footstool, leaping over scorpions and crocodiles, and [the application of] oil and ointments.
Repeatedly seizing his knives from those standing nearby, he performed various difficult feats such as the hawk’s swoop and the osprey’s dive, thereby adorning his body;
then, striking Pracaṇḍavarman— who was stationed at a distance of twenty bow-lengths— squarely in the chest with a single knife while shouting,
"May Vasantabhānu live for a thousand years!"
Having seized the thick shoulder and upper arm of a certain fierce warrior who was preparing to cut my limbs with a sword,
I rendered him senseless by that very act and caused the agitated crowd to look up in astonishment.
The wall was two men high and extremely difficult to scale.

Having leaped over it, he proceeded along the path toward the grove, saying, "This is the way seen for those following me," and thus moved along the Tamāla alley—which touched his footsteps upon its sand leveled by Nālījaṅgha—and continued along the wall;
then, having run with an imperceptible pace because the bricks were piled up again and lowered once more, he reached the base of the wall.
Having leaped over the circle of walls, ramparts,
and moats, I quickly entered that deserted monastery cell;
then, having discarded my former attire, I went with the prince to the cemetery region, where we had previously found our way through the hardships at the royal gate during the tumult of my mission.
Long before that, in that very temple of Durgā, at the very spot where the image was installed, I had prepared a cave whose outer entrance was concealed by large, firm stones set on their sides.
Then, as midnight was passing, we two—adorned with costly jeweled ornaments and silken garments brought by the eunuchs—entered that cave and remained there in silence.

The Queen, however, on the previous day itself, having provided the Malava with a funeral pyre according to his rank, and having informed Pracaṇḍavarman and Caṇḍavarman that this state of affairs was indeed caused by the treachery of the Lord of Aśmaka, sent word to them.
On the following day, at the very break of dawn, he approached together with the citizens, ministers, vassals, and elders who had been previously summoned; having worshipped the Goddess and,
while the worship was still in progress, having ensured the sanctum was secluded and closed its doors, he stood with his people, fixing his gaze upon it,
and caused a loud sound from a drum to be made.

Having been signaled by that sound which had entered through a minute opening, I lifted with my head alone the iron footstool together with the statue— a heavy object difficult to move even with the effort of stout men— and placing it on one side while supporting it with both hands, I went out; and I caused the prince to go out as well.
Then, having worshipped Durgā as before, I opened the door and appeared before them with eyes gladdened by conviction.

As the subjects prostrated themselves—hair standing on end, palms raised in reverence, and filled with wonder—I addressed them: “In this manner, the Goddess Vindhyavāsinī commands you through my mouth: ‘Today, by me, who have assumed the form of a tiger along with my attendants, [you were] overwhelmed;’”
"From this day forward, may you accept him as your own son and take him under your protection, for he is on the side of his weak mother.
Furthermore, consider me his protector— a man whose nature is harsh with deceit, made manifest by his skill in constructing millions of difficult stratagems—
and whose fee for this protection is this fair-browed sister of his, who has been granted to me by my noble lady."
Hearing this, the subjects rejoiced, saying, "Oh, how fortunate is the Bhoja dynasty, which has you, Āryadatta, as its lord!
But my mother-in-law touched a state of joy that was beyond the reach of words.
On that very day, I caused her hand, which was like a sprout, to be properly grasped by Mañjuvādinī;
and when night had fallen, I completely filled the cave.
The people, finding no opening, and employing various other means such as recounting tales of lost treasures and stolen goods, attributed my success solely to my divine nature.
He did not transgress my command.
The prince was renowned for his power because he was the son of an Ārya.
On an auspicious day, having brought him who was well-prepared, I, while having him taught political science by the domestic priest, attended to the affairs of state.
And I thought: "What is called sovereignty depends upon the three powers;
and these powers—counsel, majesty, and energy—proceed toward their tasks when mutually supported.
For by means of counsel, there is the determination of objectives."
The undertaking proceeds by means of power, and the conclusion is achieved through energy;
therefore, it is rooted in counsel consisting of five limbs.
It has a trunk consisting of two forms of power, branches of fourfold enthusiasm for the masses,
and seventy-two leaves representing the constituent elements of society.
The tree of policy (*naya-vanaspati*) of a leader, possessing the sprouts of the six qualities and bearing the flowers and fruits of power and success, provides assistance.
"And since this [kingdom] has many factions, it is difficult for one who is without allies to govern.

Now, this minister of Mitravarmā named Āryaketu, being of Kosala lineage, belongs to the faction of the prince's mother and is endowed with the qualities of a minister; having disregarded his counsel, Mitravarmā was ruined.
If he can be won over, it would be excellent."
Then he privately instructed Nālījaṅgha: “Father, speak in private to the noble Āryaketu: ‘Who is this illusory man who enjoys this royal fortune?
And yet, this child of ours has been seized by this serpent.’”
"Should it be vomited up or swallowed?
He said, "I must be informed of whatever he says.
Then he informed me of something else: "Having worshipped him repeatedly with offerings and having engaged him in various conversations,"
Having massaged his hands and feet, and having been granted a moment of great confidence, I questioned him according to the method taught by you;
she too spoke thus: "Noble sir,..."
Do not speak thus;
there is the observation of purity in his lineage,
and an extraordinary proficiency of intellect.
Superhuman vital strength,
immeasurable magnanimity,
and most marvelous skill in weaponry.
He possessed no small knowledge of the arts,
a heart moist with compassion,
and an invincible brilliance that overcame his enemies.
Thus, in him alone are gathered qualities that elsewhere are difficult to find even one by one;
he is a long-standing *bilva* tree to his enemies, but a *candana* sandalwood tree to those who bow before him.
"Having removed that one who considers himself a knower of policy, know that this prince Aśmaka has already been established in his paternal station;
let no doubt be entertained here.
Having heard this, and having repeatedly gratified him with gifts, I made him my counselor.
And as his friend, I appointed ministers endowed with truthfulness and purity, as well as secret agents disguised in various guises.
Having learned from them that the circle of subjects was generally greedy, opulent, excessively arrogant, and mostly ungovernable, I proclaimed my own lack of greed and manifested my righteousness.
Afflicting the nihilists,
clearing away thorns, and destroying the stratagems of enemies;

Establishing the four castes in their respective duties and occupations, I would have collected revenues; for undertakings distinguished by punishment are rooted in wealth, and there is nothing more wicked than that due to weakness—
having considered this, I applied myself to yogic practices.
And I thought to myself: "My entire host of servants is exceedingly brave and so devoted to me that they regard even their lives as mere straw at my command.
Furthermore, with the full military strength of two kingdoms, I am not inferior to Vasantabhanu, the Lord of Ashmaka, and I am possessed of political wisdom.
Therefore, having defeated Vasantabhanu, I am capable of establishing Bhaskaravarman—the son of Anantavarman, the King of Vidarbha—in his paternal station."
"This prince has been adopted as a son by Bhavānī,
and I have been appointed to assist him"— this rumor has spread everywhere.
Even now, no one has discovered this deception of mine.

Those stationed here have placed their hopes in this prince Bhāskaravarman, thinking, "By the grace of Bhavānī, this son of our lord Anantavarman shall obtain this kingdom. Furthermore, the army of the Lord of Aśmaka, having learned of the prince's support from Bhavānī, appears to be wavering in its resolve for battle, perceiving that "human power is not as strong as the power of the Goddess."

Moreover, the hereditary subjects here were already desirous of the prince’s elevation from the very beginning; now, having been further won over by me through gifts, honors, and various means of conciliation, they especially long for the prince alone.

Furthermore, the inner-circle servants of the Lord of Aśmaka have been made to feel great affection by my most trusted men and have been secretly instigated by my command with these words: “You are our friends; therefore, you must speak words that portend good fortune for us.”

In this matter, Her Majesty has appointed me, whose fame is well-known, to assist the prince; through my agency, she has ensured that Vasantabhauma, the King of Ashmaka, and those who stand on his side shall become guests of Death. Until the King of Ashmaka becomes an ally, you must follow Bhaskaravarman, the son of Anantavarman.

"Free from fear, having encountered a more prosperous state, he will dwell happily with his attendants, provided he does not fall under the power of Bhavānī’s trident. And Bhavānī has commanded me thus: 'Tell everyone one boon.
Therefore, perceiving your friendship, I have spoken this to all. Having heard this, those inner servants of the King of Aśmaka, learning of the prince's boon from Bhavānī, [acted] even before...
Their minds were divided;
however, upon hearing the words "mine," they all came under his control.
Having understood this entire situation, the Lord of Aśmaka thought: "All these subjects who are the hereditary followers of the prince desire none other than him as their lord."
Moreover, my external and internal circle of servants appears as if their minds are divided.
If I were to remain at home, relying on forbearance, then I would not even be able to protect my own kingdom once it has been sown with the seeds of dissension.
Therefore, while they are manifesting signs of their divided hearts to make me aware of it, let them engage in secret conversation with my forces.
Thinking, "I shall not engage in conflict with him merely because he has not yet appeared," and having resolved, "Once this is done,
he will certainly not remain before me for even a moment," he— impelled by the sin of unjustly invading another's kingdom— advanced with his army against our forces as if toward the jaws of death.
Knowing that he was approaching, the prince went forward to meet him. Thereupon, mounted upon my horse, I advanced toward the King of Aśmaka as he was coming.

At that moment, his entire army thought: "That this man alone should come against such an immeasurable host of ours—therein, surely, the grace of Bhavānī is the extraordinary cause, and nothing else."
Having resolved upon it, they remained as if painted in a picture.
Then, having approached him, I challenged Vasantabhānu to combat; he came forward and struck me forcefully with a sword-blow.
But my blow, rendered fruitless by his superior training, was countered by me as I struck back, and I severed the head of the Lord of Aśmaka.
Having struck down his soldiers in the forests, he said: "Henceforth, those who desire to fight should assemble and fight with me;
otherwise, let them prostrate at the feet of the prince, become his subjects, and dwell in peace, enjoying their respective livelihoods while fearlessly maintaining their own respective offices."
Immediately upon hearing my words, all the servants of the King of Aśmaka suddenly dismounted from their respective vehicles and, bowing before the prince, became his subordinates.

Thereupon, having entrusted that kingdom of the King of Aśmaka to the prince and appointed his hereditary ministers as officials for its protection, I arrived at Vidarbha together with the army of the King of Aśmaka, which had become my own, and [installed] that prince in the capital.
Having consecrated Bhāskaravarman, I established him in his father’s position.
Once, while that king was seated with his mother Vasundharā, I informed him: “I desire to undertake a certain task;
until it is accomplished, I am unable to remain in one place.”

"Therefore, let this wife of mine, your sister Mañjuvādinī, remain by your side for some days. And I, having wandered the earth for some time until I find my beloved, shall return here once I have found him. Having heard this, the king, with his mother's consent, said to me: "You alone are the extraordinary cause of this great prosperity of ours, characterized by the acquisition of this kingdom."
"Without you, we cannot sustain the burden of this kingdom even for a moment;
therefore, why do you speak thus? Having heard this, I replied: "You need not entertain even a trace of such anxiety in your minds.
That jewel among ministers, Āryaketu, who resides in your house, is capable of bearing the burden of many such kingdoms."

Although he was enticed by a multitude of such words as, "Therefore, having appointed him there, I shall depart," the king, together with his mother, dissuaded me from beginning my journey for some time through many persistent entreaties;
he then bestowed upon me the kingdom of Pracaṇḍavarman, the lord of Utkala.

"After I had taken that kingdom for myself and taken leave of the king, just as I was preparing to set out in search of you, I was summoned here for assistance by Siṃhavarman, the lord of Aṅga; having arrived here, I have been reunited with my master through the ripening of past merits."
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Adventures of Viśruta," in the *Daśakumāracarita* composed by Daṇḍin.
Now follows the conclusion of the story:

Then those princes who had gathered there— Apahāravarma, Upahāravarma, Arthapāla, Pramati, Mitragupta, Mantragupta, and Viśruta— were summoned by Vāmalocanā to Pāṭalipura, where they were to enjoy the status of crown prince according to a prior agreement.

Having summoned Prince Somadatta along with his wife by means of servants, the princes, together with Rājavāhana, sat down and engaged in conversations filled with mutual joy; meanwhile, royal officers arrived from Puṣpapura bearing a command-letter from King Rājahaṃsa, and having prostrated before Rājavāhana, they informed him: "O Lord,..."
Having heard, "Take this edict of King Rājahaṃsa, the progenitor," he rose, bowed repeatedly with great reverence, and received that edict in the assembly.

Placing it upon his head, then removing and unrolling it, King Rājavāhana read it aloud while everyone listened: "Hail! From the illustrious capital city of Puṣpapura, the venerable King Rājahaṃsa [addresses] Rājavāhana and the others who dwell in the city of Campā."
Having offered blessings to the princes, he sent a letter of command as follows:
"When you had taken leave of me here and departed, having bowed down, you halted your camp in a certain forest region near a temple of Śiva.
There, Rājavāhana remained in the temple at night for the purpose of worshipping Śiva; in the morning, not finding him, all the rest [of you]..."
The princes also made this vow: "We shall prostrate before Rājahaṃsa together with Rājavāhana, or else we shall give up our lives.
Having thus resolved, they turned back their army and set out separately to search for Rājavāhana.
Upon hearing this account of yours from the mouths of the soldiers who had returned, [he was cast] into an ocean of unbearable sorrow.
Both my noble-minded self and your mother, having resolved, "Let us go to the hermitage of Vāmadeva, inform him of this event,
and then renounce our lives," approached that hermitage. As soon as we had bowed to the sage and stood before him,
that sage, who knows the three periods of time, already knew our intention.
Having understood the certainty, he spoke: "O King, all this that you have desired was known from the very beginning through the power of my discernment.
As for the fact that your sons encountered misfortune for some time on account of Rājavāhana, by the dawning of their fortune and through extraordinary means—"
"Having achieved conquests in all directions through valor and acquired numerous kingdoms, they will return at the end of sixteen years, placing the victorious Rājavāhana at their head.
Having prostrated at the feet of yourself and Vasumatī, they will become executors of your commands.
Therefore, you must not commit any rash act on their account."
Having heard that, and relying on my fortitude through confidence in him, my lord and I have sustained our lives from that day forward.

Now, as the appointed time drew near, we went to the hermitage of Vāmadeva and made this representation: "Master, the period mentioned by you is nearly complete; therefore, is news of him still being learned by you?"

Having heard this, the sage said, “O King, all the princes, headed by Rājavāhana, having conquered numerous invincible enemies, performed a conquest of the quarters, and brought the circle of the earth under their control, are now stationed together in Campā.
Let servants be dispatched immediately with a letter of command from you to bring them here. Having heard these words of the sage, a letter of command has been sent to summon you.

"Therefore, if you should delay even for a moment beyond this, you will hear of me and my mother, the Earth, as nothing more than a memory. Realizing that even the water they would find on the road would have to be drunk [only after their departure], they resolved: "Carrying our father’s writ of command upon our heads, we shall go. Thus they made their decision.

Then, having appointed more capable and trustworthy men to various positions throughout the armies already established for protecting the conquered kingdom, and having secured the defense of the route with a small force, we shall defeat Mānasāra, the lord of Mālava, as previously planned,
bring that kingdom under our control, and pay homage at the feet of King Rājahaṃsa and Queen Vasumatī in Puṣpapura.
Having thus resolved, they set out toward the Lord of Mālava accompanied by their respective wives and a limited force.
Upon reaching Ujjayinī, Rājavāhana—aided by those princes as his allies and with a small army—defeated and slew the exceedingly powerful Lord of Mālava, Mānasāra, in an instant.
Then, taking his daughter Avantīsundarī, he was joined by Caṇḍavarman, the king’s former minister who had previously been imprisoned.

Having rescued Prince Puṣpodbhava along with his family and released him from captivity, they took him with them to the kingdom of the Mālava lord and brought it under their control. Then, having appointed certain ministers accompanied by troops for its protection, those princes— remaining with a limited number of soldiers— arrived at Puṣpapura, placing Rājavāhana at their head, and went before King Rājahamsa and his mother, Vasumatī.
They prostrated at his feet;
and having attained the reunion with their son, both the king and Queen Vasumatī experienced supreme joy. Then [the king spoke] to Queen Vasumatī.
Having ascertained the desire of all ten princes, headed by Rājavāhana, Vāmadeva commanded them in person: "Sirs, you shall all go once and protect your respective kingdoms with justice;
thereafter, whenever the desire arises, you must come to pay homage at the feet of your parents."

Then all those princes, placing the words of that sage upon their heads, bowed to him and to their parents; having gone forth and accomplished their conquest of the quarters, they reported their respective adventures, ending with their return, individually before the sage.
And the parents, hearing the most difficult feats performed by the princes which demonstrated their own prowess, attained supreme joy.
Then the king addressed the sage with humility: “O Blessed One, through your grace we have attained a happiness that exceeds the desires of mortal men and lies beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Therefore, it is now fitting for me to establish myself in the practice of self-realization within the forest-dweller’s stage of life (vānaprastha) in the vicinity of your holy feet.”

"Therefore, having consecrated Rājavāhana as the sovereign of Puṣpapura and the kingdom of Mānasāra, and having distributed the remaining kingdoms among the nine princes as is fitting, those princes— obeying the commands of Rājavāhana and acting with one accord— shall uproot thorns from the earth girt by the four oceans and enjoy its prosperity; thus should it be done by my lord."

Seeing their great persistence in forbidding their father’s undertaking of destroying the forest hermitage, the sage said to them: “O young men, this father of yours, while treading the path appropriate for his age, must by all means be prevented from entering my hermitage and adopting the forest-dweller’s stage of life without undergoing bodily mortification; for staying here, he will obtain devotion to the Blessed One.”

"And you shall not obtain happiness while in the presence of your father. Having received this command from the great sage, they abandoned their obstinate refusal to permit their father to enter the forest-dweller’s stage of life (*vānaprastha*).
Having established Rājavāhana in Puṣpapura, all the attendants, with his permission, governed their respective kingdoms and went to and fro at will to be near their parents.
While remaining in this state, all those princes, headed by Rājavāhana, by the command of Rājavāhana [ruled] the entire circle of the earth.
Protecting [the realm] according to justice and acting with mutual consensus, they experienced the pleasures of sovereignty— extremely difficult to obtain even for Indra and others.
Thus ends the conclusion of the story in the *Daśakumāracarita*, the work of the illustrious Daṇḍin.

Thus ends the *Daśakumāracarita* composed by the illustrious Paṇḍita Daṇḍin—the great Mahāmahopādhyāya, universal sovereign of the circle of poets, the moon to the night-lotuses of all branches of knowledge, and the very breath of Sarasvatī. It is complete.
